questions.question: A provider's attributed Medicare population has an average RAF score of 1.5. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: RAF 1.0 represents average predicted spending. RAF 1.5 means the population is predicted to cost 50% more than average — so payment targets and benchmarks are adjusted upward accordingly.

options.text: The population has 1.5 times more chronic conditions than the national average
The population is predicted to cost 50% more than an average Medicare beneficiary
The provider has submitted 1.5 HCC diagnoses per patient on average
The provider receives 150% of standard Medicare rates

lessons.title: Social Risk in Risk Adjustment: Should We Adjust for Poverty?
lessons.summary: The contested question of whether to include social risk factors in clinical quality risk adjustment — arguments on both sides and the NASEM recommendations.

objectives.text: Explain the argument for including social risk factors in quality measure risk adjustment
Explain the argument against adjusting for social risk
Summarize the NASEM recommendations on social risk adjustment

contentBlocks.heading: The core tension
contentBlocks.body:
Risk adjustment corrects for clinical complexity so that providers caring for sicker patients aren't unfairly penalized on quality or cost measures. The question: should social risk factors — poverty, housing instability, limited English proficiency — be adjusted for in the same way?

Providers argue yes: safety-net hospitals and practices caring for high-poverty populations face structural barriers to quality outcomes that have nothing to do with the quality of their care. Adjusting for social risk levels the playing field.

Equity advocates argue no: adjusting for poverty sets lower quality expectations for poor patients — essentially accepting worse care for the disadvantaged. The goal should be to close gaps, not to hide them.

contentBlocks.heading: Arguments for and against social risk adjustment

rows.label: Fairness
rows.left: Providers caring for high-social-risk patients face barriers beyond their control
rows.right: Adjustment accepts lower quality expectations for poor patients

rows.label: Access
rows.left: Without adjustment, providers may avoid high-risk populations to protect scores
rows.right: Incentives to improve social determinants may be reduced if gaps are adjusted away

rows.label: Accountability
rows.left: Penalizing safety-net providers unfairly may close them, harming access further
rows.right: Accountability requires measuring actual outcomes without excusing poor performance

contentBlocks.heading: NASEM's 2017 recommendation: stratify, don't adjust
contentBlocks.body: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) recommended stratifying quality measure results by social risk — reporting performance separately for high and low social risk patients — rather than adjusting measures to reduce apparent gaps. This preserves accountability for all providers while revealing where disparities exist. CMS has moved toward this approach.

questions.question: What did NASEM recommend for handling social risk in quality measurement?
questions.explanation: NASEM recommended stratifying quality measure results by social risk — reporting separately for high and low social risk patients — rather than adjusting measures to hide gaps.

options.text: Adjust all quality measures for social risk factors in addition to clinical risk
Stratify results by social risk to reveal disparities while preserving accountability
Exclude safety-net providers from quality measurement programs entirely
Give safety-net providers bonus payments without quality measurement requirements

tracks.title: Star Ratings & Consumer Transparency
tracks.description: How CMS Star Ratings work for Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, what's in the 5-star formula, and how Star Ratings drive plan behavior and consumer choice.

lessons.title: Medicare Advantage Star Ratings: Formula, Stakes & Strategy
lessons.summary: How CMS calculates 1-5 star ratings for Medicare Advantage plans, what the financial stakes are, and how plans manage their star strategy.

objectives.text: Explain the 5-star rating formula and its major domains
Describe the financial consequences of star rating levels for MA plans
Identify the measures with the highest weight and strategic importance

contentBlocks.heading: Stars as a market signal and a financial lever
contentBlocks.body:
CMS rates every Medicare Advantage and Part D plan on a 1–5 star scale, published annually on Medicare.gov. Stars serve two purposes: consumer transparency (beneficiaries can compare plans) and financial incentives (CMS pays quality bonuses to plans rated 4 stars or above).

The stakes are enormous. A plan earning 4+ stars receives a 5% bonus on its base payment rate — worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually for large plans. Plans below 3 stars for three consecutive years can be terminated from Medicare Advantage.

items.title: Staying healthy
items.body: Preventive screenings and vaccines — mammograms, colorectal cancer screening, flu vaccines, annual wellness visits.

items.title: Managing chronic conditions
items.body: HEDIS measures for diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol, COPD, and mental health medication adherence.

items.title: Plan responsiveness
items.body: CAHPS member experience measures — getting needed care, getting care quickly, rating of health care, customer service.

items.title: Member complaints & appeals
items.body: Complaint rates, appeals upheld, call center performance metrics.

items.title: Health plan administration
items.body: Compliance with CMS rules, pricing accuracy, and formulary compliance for Part D.

contentBlocks.heading: Highest-weight measures: where plans focus
contentBlocks.body: CMS assigns different weights to different measures — some count 3x, 4x, or 5x in the final calculation. The highest-weight measures include medication adherence for chronic conditions, care for older adults, and care transitions. Plans invest most heavily in improving these measures because the return on a star improvement is highest.

contentBlocks.label: Stars program director: what moves the needle
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a Medicare Advantage quality director about which star measures are hardest to move, what interventions have worked, and how the star program has changed plan behavior. Recommended: 8–10 minutes.

questions.question: What is the financial benefit for a Medicare Advantage plan that earns 4 or more stars?
questions.explanation: Plans rated 4+ stars receive a 5% quality bonus on their base payment rate from CMS — a significant financial incentive that drives plan investment in quality improvement.

options.text: They are exempt from network adequacy requirements
They receive a 5% quality bonus on their base payment rate
They can charge higher premiums to beneficiaries
They receive preferred status in CMS marketing materials

lessons.title: Star Ratings & Equity: The Low-Income Subsidy Problem
lessons.summary: Why Medicare Advantage plans serving high proportions of low-income and dual eligible members consistently score lower on Star Ratings — and what CMS is doing about it.

objectives.text: Explain why plans serving LIS/dual eligible populations score lower on Star Ratings
Describe the criticism that Stars penalizes safety-net MA plans
Explain how the Health Equity Index attempts to address this

contentBlocks.heading: Stars and the equity penalty
contentBlocks.body:
Research consistently shows that Medicare Advantage plans serving higher proportions of Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries and dual eligibles score lower on Star Ratings — even after controlling for plan characteristics. This creates a troubling dynamic: plans that choose to serve the most vulnerable populations are financially penalized through lower star ratings and loss of the 5% quality bonus.

Analyses by MedPAC, CMS, and academic researchers find that 20–30% of the variance in star ratings is explained by the socioeconomic composition of a plan's enrollment — not by actual quality of care delivered.

contentBlocks.heading: The Health Equity Index: CMS's response
contentBlocks.body: Starting with 2027 Star Ratings, CMS is implementing the Health Equity Index (HEI) — a reward measure that gives plans additional credit for achieving better quality outcomes for their LIS/dual eligible and/or disability members. Plans with smaller quality gaps between vulnerable and non-vulnerable members earn HEI credit. This inverts the old incentive: rather than penalizing plans for serving difficult populations, HEI rewards plans that actually close gaps within those populations.

questions.question: What is the equity concern with the current Medicare Advantage Star Ratings system?
questions.explanation: Plans serving high proportions of low-income and dual eligible members consistently score lower on Stars, losing the quality bonus — which may discourage plans from serving these populations.

options.text: Plans that serve rural populations are excluded from Star Ratings
Plans serving high proportions of low-income/dual eligible members score lower, potentially discouraging service to vulnerable populations
Star Ratings do not include measures relevant to the diseases most common in low-income populations
Low-income beneficiaries cannot compare plans on Medicare.gov

tracks.title: The Future of Value-Based Care
tracks.description: Where value-based care is heading: primary care first models, total cost of care at scale, VBC in Medicaid, and the unresolved tensions in the field.

lessons.title: Where VBC Is Heading: Primary Care, Equity & Scale
lessons.summary: The push toward primary care-centric total cost of care models, the challenge of embedding equity into VBC design, and honest assessment of what VBC has and hasn't solved.

objectives.text: Describe the AHEAD model and its significance for multi-payer VBC
Explain how VBC models can be designed to advance or inadvertently undermine equity
Articulate the honest limitations of VBC after 15 years of experimentation

contentBlocks.heading: The primary care investment deficit
contentBlocks.body: Despite 15 years of VBC, the US still underinvests in primary care relative to specialty care. Primary care receives approximately 5–7% of total health spending despite managing the majority of patient contacts. VBC models that pay for total cost of care have shown the most promise when they substantially increase primary care investment — higher per-member payments for care management, behavioral health integration, and extended access.

items.title: AHEAD Model
items.body: CMS's State All Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development (AHEAD) model. Vermont is a participant. Aligns Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers around shared total cost of care targets at the state level.

items.title: Equity in VBC
items.body: New CMS requirements for ACOs and MA plans to stratify quality data by race, ethnicity, and social risk — and to develop equity plans to close gaps.

items.title: Advanced Primary Care
items.body: CMS Primary Care First (PCF) and similar models that dramatically increase primary care revenue in exchange for total cost of care accountability.

items.title: Behavioral health integration
items.body: Collaborative Care Model payment for integrated behavioral health in primary care — finally reimbursed under CPT 99492-99494 codes.

contentBlocks.heading: What VBC has not solved
contentBlocks.body: After 15+ years of experimentation: VBC has not bent the cost curve at the population level. National health spending continues to grow faster than GDP. VBC has produced real but modest savings in specific programs. The field has learned that payment reform alone — without workforce transformation, social determinants investment, and technology alignment — is insufficient. The next chapter of VBC will need to address these structural gaps.

contentBlocks.label: Vermont's AHEAD model: a participant's view
contentBlocks.hint: Interview someone from Vermont's ACO (OneCare Vermont) or the Green Mountain Care Board about participating in the AHEAD model, what multi-payer alignment means in practice, and how Vermont's all-payer approach differs from single-payer Medicare models. Recommended: 8–12 minutes.

questions.question: What makes the AHEAD model distinct from standard ACO programs?
questions.explanation: AHEAD is a state-level multi-payer model that aligns Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers around shared total cost of care targets — unlike typical ACO programs that operate within a single payer.

options.text: AHEAD is only for rural health systems in underserved areas
AHEAD aligns multiple payers at the state level around shared total cost of care targets
AHEAD replaces Medicare Advantage in participating states
AHEAD focuses exclusively on behavioral health and substance use

lessons.title: Global Budgets for Hospitals: Maryland & Beyond
lessons.summary: How global hospital budgets set annual spending targets that decouple hospital revenue from volume — the Maryland Model, Vermont, and the evidence on cost and quality.

objectives.text: Explain what a global budget is and how it differs from capitation or fee-for-service
Describe Maryland's all-payer hospital global budget model and its results
Explain how global budgets change hospital incentives around volume and prevention

contentBlocks.heading: The hospital volume problem
contentBlocks.body:
In fee-for-service, hospitals earn revenue when patients are admitted. They lose revenue when patients avoid hospitalization — through better primary care, prevention, or care management. Global budgets fundamentally change this: a hospital receives a fixed annual budget regardless of how many patients it admits. If it can keep patients healthy and out of the hospital, it keeps the budget. If volume rises above target, it must absorb the additional cost.

This is the most complete form of hospital payment reform — aligning hospital financial incentives with population health for the first time.

contentBlocks.heading: Maryland: the only all-payer global budget state
contentBlocks.body:
Maryland has had a unique hospital payment system since 1977. The Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) sets hospital rates for all payers — Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial — under a federal waiver. In 2014, Maryland entered the Total Cost of Care Model, adding a population-level global budget for Medicare spending across all care settings.

Results after 5 years: Maryland hospitals generated $1.2B in Medicare savings, achieved lower per-capita cost growth than national trends, and showed quality improvements — particularly in preventable hospitalizations and readmissions. Vermont's AHEAD model, which Vermont entered in 2024, is modeled partly on Maryland's approach.

title: Health Equity & SDOH: From Awareness to Action
subtitle: Disparity data, SDOH screening, algorithmic bias, CMS equity requirements, and community-level change
description: A rigorous course on health equity and social determinants of health — moving beyond awareness into measurement, accountability, and action. Covers disparity data, SDOH screening tools, algorithmic bias in clinical AI, CMS equity mandates, structural racism in the health system, and community health worker models. Relevant for every role in health care and policy.
targetAudience: Managed care and value-based care staff

tracks.title: Foundations of Health Equity
tracks.description: Definitions, the distinction between equality and equity, the evidence on disparities, and why the US performs worse on equity than peer nations.

lessons.title: Health Equity: Definitions, Evidence & the US Context
lessons.summary: What health equity means, the difference between disparity and inequity, the scale of US health disparities, and the evidence that they are not inevitable.

objectives.text: Define health equity and distinguish it from equality and diversity
Describe the scale of racial, socioeconomic, and geographic health disparities in the US
Explain why health disparities are considered unjust rather than inevitable

contentBlocks.heading: What health equity means — and what it doesn't
contentBlocks.body:
Health equity means that everyone has a fair and just opportunity to be as healthy as possible. It requires removing obstacles to health — poverty, discrimination, inadequate housing, unsafe neighborhoods, poor education — that systematically disadvantage certain groups.

Health equity is not the same as health equality. Equality means giving everyone the same thing. Equity means giving people what they need, which differs based on their circumstances. A useful illustration: three people of different heights trying to watch a game over a fence. Equality gives each person one box. Equity gives the shortest person two boxes, the tallest none — so everyone can see.

Health equity is also not the same as diversity, inclusion, or belonging — though these are related. Equity is specifically about outcomes and the conditions that produce them.

stats.label: Life expectancy gap between Black and white Americans (2023)
Higher maternal mortality rate for Black women vs. white women
Higher infant mortality for babies born to Black mothers vs. white mothers in some states
Life expectancy gap between richest and poorest US counties

contentBlocks.heading: Disparity vs. inequity: a critical distinction
contentBlocks.body: Not all disparities are inequities. A disparity is any measurable difference between groups. An inequity is a disparity that is unjust and avoidable — the result of systemic disadvantage rather than biology or free choice. Framing matters: calling disparities 'inequities' assigns moral weight and implies action. Research increasingly shows that most racial health disparities are not explained by biology but by social and structural factors.

contentBlocks.caption: What is health equity? — RWJF foundational explainer (~5 min)

contentBlocks.heading: The Whitehall Study: status, not just poverty
contentBlocks.body: The British Whitehall Studies (1960s–1980s) followed civil servants across salary grades. Even controlling for lifestyle factors, higher-grade civil servants had dramatically better health outcomes than lower-grade ones — and this gradient held at every rung, not just at the bottom. Health disadvantage is not only about poverty; it tracks social status, power, and control throughout the socioeconomic ladder.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between a health 'disparity' and a health 'inequity'?
questions.explanation: A disparity is any measurable difference between groups. An inequity is a disparity that is unjust and avoidable — produced by systemic disadvantage rather than biology or free choice.

options.text: Disparities are differences by race; inequities are differences by income
An inequity is a disparity that is unjust and avoidable, caused by systemic disadvantage
Inequities are larger in magnitude than disparities
Disparities exist in clinical care; inequities exist in social systems outside health care

questions.question: By approximately how much does life expectancy differ between the richest and poorest US counties?

options.text: About 5 years
About 10 years
About 20 years
About 2 years

lessons.title: Structural Racism & Health: From Redlining to Clinical Bias
lessons.summary: How structural racism — through housing, education, wealth, and clinical practice — produces health disparities, and what the evidence says about implicit bias in clinical settings.

objectives.text: Explain how structural racism — not just individual prejudice — produces health disparities
Describe the health effects of discriminatory housing policy (redlining)
Summarize the evidence on implicit bias in clinical settings

contentBlocks.heading: Beyond individual prejudice
contentBlocks.body:
When people hear 'racism,' they often think of individual bigotry — explicit prejudice held by a specific person. Structural racism is different: it refers to the historical and ongoing policies, practices, and norms that systematically advantage some groups and disadvantage others, often without any individual intending harm.

Health disparities are largely the product of structural racism: differential access to wealth, education, housing, environmental quality, and safety — all of which are powerful determinants of health — that have been shaped by policy decisions across generations.

contentBlocks.heading: Redlining and health: the maps still matter
contentBlocks.body:
From the 1930s through the 1960s, the federal government's Home Owners' Loan Corporation drew color-coded maps of US cities, rating neighborhoods for lending risk. Neighborhoods with Black residents were systematically marked red ('hazardous') — denying mortgages that would have built intergenerational wealth.

Researchers have overlaid 1930s redlining maps on modern health data and found persistent correlations: formerly redlined neighborhoods today have higher rates of asthma, diabetes, hypertension, low birth weight, and shorter life expectancy — 80+ years after the maps were drawn. The mechanism is through concentrated poverty, disinvestment, environmental hazard siting, and stress.

contentBlocks.heading: Implicit bias in clinical settings
contentBlocks.body: Dozens of studies document disparities in pain management, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment recommendations that persist after controlling for clinical variables. Black patients receive less pain medication than white patients with identical presentations. Studies using identical vignettes with patient names swapped show different treatment recommendations based on perceived race. This is not conscious racism — it reflects unconscious associations that every clinician is susceptible to, which is why training and system-level safeguards matter.

contentBlocks.label: Clinician on addressing bias in practice
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a physician or nurse about their experience encountering and addressing implicit bias in clinical settings — what they've seen, how they've changed their practice, and what systemic changes would help. Recommended: 7–10 minutes.

questions.question: What is 'structural racism' as distinct from individual prejudice?
questions.explanation: Structural racism refers to policies, practices, and norms that systematically advantage some groups and disadvantage others — often without any individual intending harm.

options.text: Racism expressed openly by people in positions of authority
Policies and practices that systematically disadvantage certain groups, often without individual intent
Racism that exists only in social systems, not in health care
Unconscious bias held by individual clinicians

lessons.title: The US in Global Context: Why We Spend More and Get Less
lessons.summary: How the US compares to peer nations on health outcomes — life expectancy, maternal mortality, infant mortality — despite spending twice as much, and what drives the gap.

objectives.text: Compare US health outcomes to peer OECD nations on key indicators
Explain why the US spends more per capita but achieves worse outcomes
Identify which US populations drive the worst outcome gaps

contentBlocks.heading: The paradox: most spending, worst outcomes
contentBlocks.body:
The United States spends approximately $12,500 per person per year on health care — more than twice the average of other high-income OECD nations. Yet the US ranks last or near-last among OECD countries on life expectancy, maternal mortality, infant mortality, and chronic disease burden.

This is not primarily a question of health care quality for those who access it — US care for insured patients with good access is among the best in the world. It is a question of who gets access, and the profound health consequences of leaving tens of millions of people uninsured, underinsured, or under-resourced.

stats.label: US per capita health spending (2022) — highest in the world
US life expectancy (2022) — below all peer nations
US maternal mortality per 100,000 — 3x higher than UK, France, Canada
US infant mortality per 1,000 — highest among comparable nations

contentBlocks.heading: The American Health Disadvantage is not uniform
contentBlocks.body: A 2013 National Academies study ('Shorter Lives, Poorer Health') found that the US health disadvantage is concentrated in specific populations: uninsured, low-income, Black and Hispanic Americans drive most of the gap with peer nations. White, college-educated, insured Americans have health outcomes roughly comparable to their counterparts in other countries. The overall US underperformance is a story of who is left behind.

contentBlocks.caption: Why is US healthcare so expensive? — Vox explainer (~8 min)

questions.question: According to the 2013 National Academies 'Shorter Lives, Poorer Health' study, the US health disadvantage is primarily concentrated in which groups?
questions.explanation: The study found the disadvantage concentrated in uninsured, low-income, and racial/ethnic minority Americans — white, college-educated, insured Americans have outcomes comparable to peer nations.

options.text: All Americans, uniformly across income and racial groups
Uninsured, low-income, and racial/ethnic minority populations
Primarily elderly Americans above age 75
Rural Americans regardless of income or insurance

tracks.title: Social Determinants of Health
tracks.description: The evidence on SDOH, the five Healthy People domains, how SDOH screening works in clinical settings, and the Z-codes used to document social needs.

lessons.title: The Evidence on SDOH: What Drives Health More Than Health Care
lessons.summary: Why social determinants account for more of health outcomes than clinical care, the five Healthy People 2030 SDOH domains, and the strongest SDOH-health linkages.

objectives.text: Explain the relative contribution of SDOH vs. clinical care to health outcomes
Describe the five Healthy People 2030 SDOH domains
Identify the strongest evidence-based links between specific SDOH and health outcomes

contentBlocks.heading: 30% clinical care, 70% everything else
contentBlocks.body:
The most widely cited estimate in health equity work: clinical care accounts for approximately 10–20% of health outcomes. The remaining 80–90% is shaped by social and economic factors, health behaviors, and environment.

This doesn't mean health care doesn't matter — it does, especially in acute crisis. But it does mean that a health system laser-focused on clinical quality while ignoring where patients live, work, eat, and breathe is optimizing the wrong variable.

items.title: Education access & quality
items.body: Educational attainment is one of the strongest predictors of health. More education → higher income, better jobs, better health literacy, longer life.

items.title: Economic stability
items.body: Income, employment, food security, housing stability. Poverty is a powerful health risk factor — both through material deprivation and chronic stress.

items.title: Social & community context
items.body: Social support, discrimination, community cohesion, civic participation. Social isolation is comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes/day for health impact.

items.title: Health care access & quality
items.body: Insurance coverage, geographic access to providers, quality of care received, health literacy, and trust in health care systems.

items.title: Neighborhood & built environment
items.body: Housing quality, air and water quality, access to healthy food, walkability, safety. ZIP code predicts health better than genetic code.

lessons.title: SDOH Screening in Clinical Settings: Tools, Z-Codes & Referrals
lessons.summary: How clinical teams screen for social needs using validated tools (PRAPARE, AHC, SEEK), document with ICD-10 Z-codes, and connect patients to community resources.

objectives.text: Identify validated SDOH screening tools and their appropriate use cases
Explain how Z-codes are used to document social needs in clinical records
Describe the closed-loop referral model for connecting patients to community resources

contentBlocks.heading: Screening: from asking to acting
contentBlocks.body:
SDOH screening asks patients about their social needs directly — food security, housing stability, transportation, utilities, interpersonal safety. The evidence shows patients are willing to answer these questions when asked in a respectful, confidential context, and that screening identifies needs that clinicians would not otherwise know about.

But screening without action causes harm: asking someone if they're food insecure and then having no response to offer erodes trust. Effective SDOH programs pair screening with a referral pathway — either through embedded community health workers, a care coordination team, or a community resource platform like findhelp or NowPow.

items.title: PRAPARE
items.body: Protocol for Responding to and Assessing Patients' Assets, Risks, and Experiences. 21-item tool from NACHC. Maps to Z-codes. Most widely used in FQHCs.

items.title: AHC Screening Tool
items.body: Accountable Health Communities screening tool developed by CMS. 10 core questions covering food, housing, transportation, utilities, and safety. Required for CMS AHC model participants.

items.title: SEEK
items.body: Safe Environment for Every Kid. Pediatric tool designed for primary care. Screens for family stress, substance use, depression, and food insecurity during well-child visits.

items.title: SDOH-5
items.body: Brief 5-question tool for rapid screening in high-volume settings. Covers food, housing, transportation, interpersonal violence, and utilities.

contentBlocks.heading: Z-codes: documenting social needs in ICD-10
contentBlocks.body:
ICD-10-CM Z-codes (in the Z55–Z65 range) capture social determinants of health in clinical documentation:

- Z59.0: Homelessness
- Z59.4: Lack of adequate food
- Z63.0: Problems in relationship with spouse or partner
- Z56.0: Unemployment, unspecified
- Z60.2: Problems related to living alone

Z-codes enable population-level analysis of social needs in a practice or system, support quality reporting, and increasingly are used by payers to adjust risk scores and target interventions. Documentation of Z-codes has historically been low — many clinicians don't know they exist or don't realize the clinical and operational value of using them.

contentBlocks.heading: Closed-loop referrals: did the patient get help?
contentBlocks.body: A warm referral to a food bank is better than a pamphlet. A closed-loop referral — where the receiving organization confirms the patient connected with services and sends that information back to the care team — is better still. Community resource platforms like findhelp (formerly Aunt Bertha), NowPow, and Unite Us are building the infrastructure for closed-loop referrals at scale.

questions.question: What are ICD-10 Z-codes (Z55–Z65) used for in clinical settings?
questions.explanation: Z-codes in this range are used to document social determinants of health in clinical records — capturing social needs like homelessness, food insecurity, and unemployment for population analysis and quality reporting.

options.text: To document vaccination status for public health reporting
To document social determinants of health like food insecurity and housing instability
To code for mental health diagnoses under DSM-5
To flag patients who are uninsured or underinsured

lessons.title: Housing as Health Care: Homelessness, Eviction & the Medical Costs
lessons.summary: The evidence linking housing instability to health outcomes, what happens medically when people lose housing, and how health systems are beginning to pay for housing as a health intervention.

objectives.text: Describe the health consequences of housing instability and homelessness
Explain the Housing First model and the evidence for its effectiveness
Describe how Medicaid and ACO models are beginning to pay for housing-related services

contentBlocks.heading: Housing is health care
contentBlocks.body:
Housing instability — eviction risk, overcrowding, unsafe conditions, or outright homelessness — is one of the strongest predictors of poor health outcomes. People experiencing homelessness have life expectancies 20–25 years shorter than housed people. They use emergency departments at rates 5–10 times higher than the general population, are hospitalized more frequently, and have dramatically higher rates of mental illness, substance use, and communicable disease.

For health systems operating in value-based contracts, chronically unhoused patients are often the highest-cost, hardest-to-manage members of the population. Housing instability is not a social problem on the side — it is a primary driver of health care costs.

items.title: Housing First
items.body: Provides permanent housing to chronically homeless people immediately, without requiring sobriety or treatment compliance first. Strong RCT evidence: higher housing retention, comparable or better health outcomes than treatment-first models.

items.title: Medical respite
items.body: Short-term residential care for medically ill people experiencing homelessness who don't require hospital level care. Reduces inappropriate ED use and readmissions.

items.title: Medicaid housing supports
items.body: CMS now allows Medicaid to pay for tenancy support services, housing navigation, and transitional rent for high-need populations through 1115 waivers.

items.title: Health system investment
items.body: Some health systems (Kaiser, Dignity Health, Boston Medical Center) have invested directly in affordable housing — treating it as a population health investment that reduces their most expensive utilization.

questions.question: What is the core principle of the Housing First model?
questions.explanation: Housing First provides permanent housing immediately without requiring sobriety, treatment, or compliance as a precondition — based on evidence that stable housing enables better treatment engagement than treatment-first approaches.

options.text: Housing is provided after 90 days of sobriety and compliance with treatment
Permanent housing is provided immediately, without preconditions like sobriety

lessons.title: Food Insecurity & Health: From Screening to Prescription
lessons.summary: The health consequences of food insecurity, how clinical teams screen and respond, and the growing produce prescription and medically tailored meal programs in value-based care.

objectives.text: Describe the health consequences of food insecurity beyond hunger
Explain produce prescription and medically tailored meal programs and their evidence
Describe SNAP's role in food security and its limitations as a health intervention

contentBlocks.heading: Food insecurity is a clinical issue
contentBlocks.body:
Food insecurity — limited or uncertain access to adequate food — affects approximately 44 million Americans, including 13 million children. For clinicians, food insecurity is not just a social problem: it is directly linked to uncontrolled diabetes (food-insecure patients have 27% higher A1c), hypertension, depression, and hospital readmissions.

A diabetic patient who cannot afford or access fresh vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein cannot manage their blood sugar regardless of how good their medication is. Food is medicine — and clinicians are increasingly recognizing that prescriptions for metformin need to be paired with access to food.

items.title: Produce prescriptions
items.body: Clinicians write 'prescriptions' redeemable at farmers markets or grocery stores for fresh produce. RCTs show A1c reductions of 0.6–1.0% in food-insecure diabetic patients.

items.title: Medically tailored meals
items.body: Home-delivered meals designed by registered dietitians for specific conditions (diabetes, CHF, renal disease, HIV). Strong evidence: 50% reduction in hospitalizations in some studies.

items.title: Food pharmacy
items.body: Grocery-store-style areas within clinical settings where food-insecure patients can 'shop' for free healthy food. Pioneer sites: Boston Medical Center, Geisinger.

items.title: SNAP enrollment
items.body: Clinical teams screen for SNAP eligibility and connect patients. Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program covers ~$200/month in food for eligible individuals — but only 82% of eligible people are enrolled.

Higher A1c in food-insecure vs. food-secure diabetic patients
Reduction in hospitalizations with medically tailored meals in some studies
Of eligible people not enrolled in SNAP

questions.question: What have clinical trials found about produce prescription programs for food-insecure diabetic patients?
questions.explanation: RCTs of produce prescription programs show A1c reductions of 0.6–1.0% in food-insecure diabetic patients — clinically meaningful reductions comparable to adding a medication.

options.text: No clinical impact — A1c is not affected by diet alone
A1c reductions of 0.6–1.0% — comparable to adding a medication
Improved patient satisfaction but no measurable A1c change

tracks.title: Measuring & Reporting Disparities
tracks.description: How to collect, stratify, and act on race, ethnicity, and language (REaL) data, and the role of disparity measurement in quality programs.

lessons.title: REaL Data: Collecting Race, Ethnicity & Language
lessons.summary: Why REaL data collection is foundational to equity work, common pitfalls in collection, and how stratified quality reporting reveals disparities invisible in aggregate data.

objectives.text: Explain why high-quality REaL data collection is foundational to equity measurement
Identify common failures in REaL data collection and how to address them
Explain how stratified quality reporting reveals disparities hidden in aggregate data

contentBlocks.heading: You can't improve what you don't measure
contentBlocks.body:
The single most common reason health systems cannot identify disparities in their own care is data quality. Race and ethnicity data is frequently missing, miscategorized, or so coarsely collected (five broad categories) that meaningful analysis is impossible.

High-quality REaL data collection — asking patients directly, using the full OMB category set, collecting preferred language separately from ethnicity — is the prerequisite for everything else in equity work. You cannot stratify quality measures, set improvement targets, or demonstrate progress without it.

contentBlocks.heading: Common REaL data problems and solutions

rows.label: Race
rows.right: Self-reported by patient at registration or via patient portal

rows.label: Ethnicity
rows.left: Collapsed into race (Hispanic listed as a race)
rows.right: Collected separately: ethnicity (Hispanic/Not Hispanic) AND race

rows.label: Detail
rows.right: Granular sub-categories (e.g., Cambodian, Dominican, Somali) within OMB categories

rows.label: Language
rows.left: Not collected or conflated with ethnicity
rows.right: Preferred spoken language AND preferred written language collected separately

rows.label: Missing data
rows.right: Protocols to request self-identification at next encounter

contentBlocks.heading: The aggregate trap
contentBlocks.body: A hospital's colorectal cancer screening rate is 72% — at or above the national average. Looks fine. But stratified by race: white patients 79%, Black patients 61%, Hispanic patients 54%. The aggregate hides a 25-point gap. This is the aggregate trap: good overall performance can mask severe disparities. Equity work requires stratified measurement.

contentBlocks.label: Health system equity analyst: building the data infrastructure
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a data analyst or quality leader at a health system about the practical challenges of collecting and using REaL data — EHR limitations, staff training, patient trust. Recommended: 7–9 minutes.

questions.question: What is the 'aggregate trap' in quality measurement?
questions.explanation: The aggregate trap occurs when good overall (aggregate) performance hides severe disparities between subgroups — making stratified measurement essential.

options.text: Collecting too much data from too many patients, causing analysis paralysis
Good aggregate quality scores that hide significant disparities between demographic subgroups
Using population averages to set individual patient treatment goals
Failing to collect data on patients who decline to self-identify

lessons.title: From Disparity Data to Equity Action Plans
lessons.summary: Once you have stratified disparity data, what do you do with it? Building equity action plans, setting improvement targets, designing targeted interventions, and measuring progress.

objectives.text: Describe the structure of an equity action plan
Explain how to select targeted interventions for identified disparity gaps
Identify how health systems can set measurable equity improvement targets

contentBlocks.heading: Data is necessary but not sufficient
contentBlocks.body:
Health systems that successfully reduce disparities share a common pattern: they move rapidly from data (showing the gap exists) to action (designing and deploying targeted interventions) to accountability (tracking progress and tying leadership goals to equity outcomes).

The systems that stall are those that use data collection as a destination rather than a starting point — producing beautiful dashboards of disparity without organizational commitment to close them.

items.title: Identify the gap
items.body: Stratify a key quality measure (e.g., postpartum follow-up) by race/ethnicity. Quantify the gap between highest and lowest performing groups.

items.title: Understand the root cause
items.body: Disaggregate further: Is the gap in scheduling? No-show rates? Appointment availability? Provider distribution? Root cause determines the right intervention.

items.title: Design the intervention
items.body: Evidence-based options: CHW outreach to the gap population, language concordant appointment scheduling, reminder calls in preferred language, same-day appointments.

items.title: Set the target
items.body: Specific, measurable, time-bound: 'Reduce the Black-white postpartum follow-up gap from 18 points to 8 points within 18 months.'

items.title: Measure and iterate
items.body: Monthly tracking against target. If the gap is not closing, revisit root cause analysis. Treat disparity reduction like any quality improvement project.

contentBlocks.heading: Tie leadership goals to equity outcomes
contentBlocks.body: Health systems that make measurable progress on equity consistently tie senior leader performance goals — and compensation — to equity metrics. When the CEO's and CMO's annual reviews include a measurable equity goal, the organization allocates resources, attention, and accountability to closing it. Systems that treat equity as a values statement without accountability rarely make measurable progress.

questions.question: What is the most important factor that distinguishes health systems making measurable equity progress from those that stall?
questions.explanation: Research on high-performing equity health systems consistently finds that tying leadership performance and compensation to equity metrics is the key driver of organizational change — not just having data.

options.text: Having the most sophisticated data dashboards and analytics infrastructure
Tying senior leadership goals and compensation to measurable equity outcomes
Receiving extra CMS funding designated for equity improvement
Having a majority-minority patient population that creates urgency

tracks.title: Algorithmic Bias in Healthcare
tracks.description: How clinical algorithms and AI tools can encode and amplify health disparities, landmark cases of biased algorithms, and frameworks for bias evaluation.

lessons.title: Algorithmic Bias: When Automation Amplifies Disparity
lessons.summary: How clinical risk scores and AI tools can perpetuate and amplify racial disparities — the kidney function (eGFR) case, the Optum care management algorithm, and what health systems can do.

objectives.text: Explain how training data and design choices can encode bias into clinical algorithms
Describe two landmark cases of biased clinical algorithms and their consequences
Identify key questions health systems should ask when evaluating a clinical algorithm

contentBlocks.heading: Automation is not neutrality
contentBlocks.body:
There is a widespread assumption that algorithms and AI are more objective than human judgment. This is false. Algorithms trained on historical data inherit the biases embedded in that data. Algorithms designed without equity analysis can produce outputs that discriminate — consistently and at scale — without any human intending it.

The consequences in healthcare are serious: algorithms that guide who gets care management, who gets referred to specialists, whose pain is taken seriously, or who qualifies for transplant — all can amplify existing disparities if not carefully designed and evaluated.

contentBlocks.heading: Case 1: The kidney function algorithm (eGFR)
contentBlocks.body:
For decades, the standard formula for estimating kidney function (eGFR — estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate) included a 'race correction': it assigned Black patients higher scores, estimating that Black patients had higher baseline kidney function.

The consequence: Black patients' kidney function was systematically overestimated. They appeared healthier on paper than they were, which delayed referrals to nephrologists, delayed transplant evaluation, and resulted in Black patients being sicker when they were finally listed for kidney transplants.

In 2021, NKF and ASN recommended eliminating race from the eGFR equation. Most major health systems have adopted race-free eGFR. This is a case where the algorithm encoded a contested biological assumption that turned out to be wrong — and caused measurable harm.

contentBlocks.heading: Case 2: The Optum care management algorithm
contentBlocks.body:
A 2019 Science paper analyzed an algorithm used by Optum (and widely licensed to health systems) to identify patients who should be enrolled in high-touch care management programs. The algorithm used *healthcare costs* as a proxy for health needs — patients who had spent the most were predicted to need the most care.

The problem: Black patients, on average, spend less on health care than white patients with the same health needs — because of less access, less trust, and systemic undertreatment. By using costs as a proxy for needs, the algorithm systematically underidentified Black patients as eligible for care management. Among patients the algorithm flagged as high-need, only 17.7% were Black — when their true share by health status should have been 46.5%.

contentBlocks.heading: Questions to ask when evaluating a clinical algorithm
contentBlocks.body:
1. What data was this trained on? Does the training data reflect historical inequities?
2. Was the algorithm's performance validated separately for different racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic groups?
3. What proxy measures does it use — and are those proxies distributed differently across groups?
4. Who is the algorithm designed to help, and who might it systematically disadvantage?
5. Is there an ongoing bias monitoring protocol after deployment?

contentBlocks.caption: Algorithmic bias in healthcare — STAT News and Harvard explainer (~8 min)

questions.question: What was the equity problem with the Optum care management algorithm identified in the 2019 Science paper?
questions.explanation: The algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs. Since Black patients spent less on healthcare than white patients with the same health needs (due to barriers to access), the algorithm systematically underidentified Black patients for care management.

options.text: The algorithm used race as an explicit input, which was illegal
Using healthcare costs as a proxy for needs underidentified Black patients, who spent less despite similar health needs
The algorithm was only trained on white patients and had no data on Black patients
Black patients were enrolled at higher rates than appropriate, reducing resources for white patients

lessons.title: Pulse Oximetry & Hidden Bias in Medical Devices
lessons.summary: How pulse oximeters were found to overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin — causing delayed COVID treatment — and what it reveals about device development and equity.

objectives.text: Explain how pulse oximetry bias was identified and its clinical consequences
Describe how the bias was introduced through device development and validation
Explain FDA's response and the broader lesson for medical device equity

contentBlocks.heading: A trusted device that wasn't equally accurate
contentBlocks.body:
Pulse oximeters — the small clip devices that measure blood oxygen saturation — have been ubiquitous in clinical care for decades. During COVID-19, they were essential: the decision to admit a patient or discharge them often hinged on a single SpO2 reading.

In 2020–2021, multiple studies published in NEJM and other leading journals found that pulse oximeters were significantly less accurate in patients with darker skin tones — overestimating oxygen saturation by 2–3 percentage points. This meant that Black and Hispanic patients with dangerously low oxygen levels appeared to be within normal range, leading to delayed treatment and worse outcomes.

This was not a COVID-era discovery — the bias had been documented in the 1980s and 1990s, but the clinical and regulatory systems failed to act on it.

contentBlocks.heading: Why the bias exists — and was ignored
contentBlocks.body: Pulse oximeters work by shining light through the finger and measuring absorption at two wavelengths. Melanin in the skin absorbs light at these wavelengths, interfering with the measurement. Device manufacturers validated their devices predominantly on lighter-skinned subjects — a common pattern in medical device and clinical trial populations. Despite early research flagging the disparity, the FDA did not require manufacturers to validate accuracy across skin tones until 2024.

stats.label: Higher rate of occult hypoxemia in Black patients missed by pulse oximetry vs. white patients
Average SpO2 overestimation in patients with darker skin tones
Year FDA first required manufacturers to validate pulse oximeters across skin tones

questions.question: Why do standard pulse oximeters tend to overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin?
questions.explanation: Melanin absorbs light at the same wavelengths pulse oximeters use to measure oxygen saturation, interfering with the measurement and producing falsely high readings in patients with more melanin.

options.text: Dark skin reflects more light, causing the device to read higher values
Melanin absorbs light at the measurement wavelengths, interfering with accuracy
The bias is not in the device but in how clinicians interpret readings
Patients with darker skin have inherently higher baseline oxygen saturation

tracks.title: CMS Equity Requirements & Policy
tracks.description: CMS's health equity strategy, the Health Equity Index in Star Ratings, Section 1557 non-discrimination, and the ACA's equity-related provisions.

lessons.title: CMS Health Equity Strategy: From Aspiration to Requirement
lessons.summary: CMS's Framework for Health Equity, the Health Equity Index in Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, AHEAD model equity requirements, and Section 1557 non-discrimination obligations.

objectives.text: Describe the five priorities in CMS's Framework for Health Equity
Explain how the Health Equity Index affects Medicare Advantage Star Ratings
Summarize Section 1557 non-discrimination obligations for health care organizations

contentBlocks.heading: From voluntary to required
contentBlocks.body: Health equity has moved from a voluntary aspiration to a regulatory requirement. CMS has embedded equity into payment programs, quality reporting, and plan contracting in ways that give health systems and payers financial and legal incentives to close disparities — not just acknowledge them.

contentBlocks.heading: CMS Framework for Health Equity — 5 priorities

items.title: Data collection
items.body: Expand collection of REaL and SDOH data across all CMS programs and require stratified reporting.

items.title: Underserved communities
items.body: Assess and address barriers to participation by underserved communities in CMS programs.

items.title: Disparities research
items.body: Build evidence on interventions that close disparities and share findings with the field.

items.title: Payment models
items.body: Embed equity in payment models — including requiring disparity reduction plans in ACO and APM contracts.

items.title: Cultural competency
items.body: Ensure CMS-funded organizations provide culturally and linguistically appropriate services (CLAS standards).

contentBlocks.heading: Health Equity Index in Star Ratings
contentBlocks.body: Beginning with the 2027 Star Ratings, CMS is introducing a Health Equity Index (HEI) reward that gives Medicare Advantage plans additional credit for improving quality for low-income and/or disabled enrollees. Plans that reduce disparities within their enrolled population are rewarded; those that perform worse for vulnerable subgroups are penalized. This is the first time equity performance has been directly linked to MA payment.

contentBlocks.heading: Section 1557: Non-discrimination in health care
contentBlocks.body:
Section 1557 of the ACA prohibits discrimination based on race, color, national origin, sex, age, and disability by any health program or activity receiving federal financial assistance — which includes virtually every hospital, health system, and insurer.

The 2024 Section 1557 final rule extended protections to LGBTQ+ individuals, required covered entities to provide meaningful access for people with limited English proficiency, and established requirements for accessible communication for people with disabilities. Health systems with federal funding must have a designated coordinator, a grievance procedure, and notice of nondiscrimination posted.

questions.question: What does CMS's Health Equity Index in Medicare Advantage Star Ratings reward?
questions.explanation: The Health Equity Index gives additional Star Rating credit to MA plans that demonstrate better quality performance for low-income and/or disabled enrollees — tying equity performance directly to payment.

options.text: Plans that serve a higher percentage of racial minority enrollees
Plans that improve quality for low-income and/or disabled enrollees relative to their overall performance
Plans that hire a higher percentage of minority clinical staff
Plans that partner with Federally Qualified Health Centers

lessons.title: CLAS Standards & Language Access: Legal Requirements & Best Practices
lessons.summary: The National CLAS Standards, the legal right to language access under Section 1557, and what health systems must do to serve patients with limited English proficiency.

objectives.text: Describe the National CLAS Standards and their structure
Explain the legal obligations for language access under Section 1557
Identify best practices for providing language access beyond legal minimums

contentBlocks.heading: Language is a social determinant of health
contentBlocks.body:
Approximately 25 million Americans have limited English proficiency (LEP). These patients are less likely to receive preventive care, more likely to experience medication errors, less likely to understand discharge instructions, and more likely to be readmitted. Language barriers have been linked to worse patient safety outcomes across multiple studies.

Federal law (Section 1557 of the ACA, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act) requires health care organizations receiving federal funding to provide meaningful access to patients with LEP — at no cost to the patient. This means qualified interpreters, not family members or staff who happen to speak the language.

contentBlocks.heading: The National CLAS Standards — key principals

items.title: Language services
items.body: Provide language assistance to patients with LEP at all points of contact — clinical care, registration, billing, patient education. At no cost to the patient.

items.title: Culturally competent care
items.body: Integrate cultural and linguistic responsiveness into governance, leadership, and workforce. Train staff in cultural humility.

items.title: Diverse workforce
items.body: Recruit, retain, and promote diverse staff and leadership that reflects the communities served.

items.title: Community engagement
items.body: Partner with communities served, especially underserved, to design and evaluate services.

contentBlocks.heading: Family interpreters: convenient but dangerous
contentBlocks.body: Using family members, friends, or untrained bilingual staff as interpreters is a legal and safety risk. Family members may filter information (especially around bad news or sensitive topics), lack medical vocabulary, misinterpret clinical terms, and create privacy violations. Section 1557 requires qualified interpreters — professional in-person, telephone, or video remote interpreting. The convenience of using a patient's child as an interpreter does not outweigh these risks.

questions.question: Under Section 1557 and the CLAS Standards, can a health system use a patient's family member as an interpreter to meet language access requirements?
questions.explanation: Family members are generally not acceptable as interpreters under federal law — they may filter information, lack medical vocabulary, and create privacy risks. Qualified interpreters (in-person, telephone, or video) are required.

options.text: Yes, if the patient signs a waiver agreeing to use a family member
No, qualified interpreters are required — family members are generally not acceptable
Yes, if no professional interpreter is available within 30 minutes
Yes, for routine appointments but not for consent or discharge conversations

tracks.title: Community Health Workers & Community Action
tracks.description: The evidence on community health workers, how to build CHW programs, cross-sector partnerships, and the role of community in health equity transformation.

lessons.title: Community Health Workers: Evidence, Roles & Sustainability
lessons.summary: The evidence base for CHW programs, the specific roles CHWs play in bridging clinical and community systems, Medicaid CHW reimbursement, and program design principles.

objectives.text: Describe the core roles of community health workers and what makes them effective
Summarize the evidence on CHW impact on utilization, outcomes, and equity
Explain how states are financing CHW programs through Medicaid

contentBlocks.heading: The trusted bridge
contentBlocks.body:
Community health workers are lay health workers — typically from the same community they serve — who bridge the gap between clinical health systems and the communities they struggle to reach. They are known by many names: promotoras, navigators, health coaches, patient advocates.

What makes CHWs effective is not primarily their knowledge (though training matters) but their trust. A CHW who shares the language, culture, and lived experience of the patients they serve can build relationships that clinical staff — however well-intentioned — often cannot.

items.title: Navigation
items.body: Help patients navigate complex health and social service systems — appointments, insurance enrollment, benefits applications.

items.title: Social needs
items.body: Connect patients with food, housing, transportation, and financial assistance. The direct link between SDOH screening and resource connection.

items.title: Chronic disease support
items.body: Support self-management for diabetes, hypertension, asthma. Evidence shows CHW support improves medication adherence and reduces A1c.

items.title: Maternal health
items.body: Doula and CHW models have demonstrated reduction in maternal mortality and disparities — particularly for Black mothers.

stats.label: Return on investment for every $1 spent on CHW programs (meta-analysis)
Reduction in ED visits in CHW-supported high-risk populations
States that now reimburse CHW services through Medicaid
Black maternal mortality reduction with doula/CHW support in some programs

contentBlocks.heading: Medicaid CHW reimbursement: the sustainability solution
contentBlocks.body: Historically, CHW programs were grant-funded — effective but fragile. More than 33 states now reimburse CHW services through Medicaid, providing a sustainable funding stream. CMS has made this easier through guidance on billing CHW services as part of chronic care management, care coordination, and preventive services. Vermont reimburses CHW services through Medicaid and has integrated CHWs into its ACO model.

contentBlocks.label: Community health worker: the view from the community
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a CHW about their day-to-day work — what they actually do, the barriers their patients face, what makes the role effective, and what the health system gets wrong about community engagement. Recommended: 8–12 minutes.

questions.question: What is the primary reason community health workers are effective in reaching underserved populations?
questions.explanation: CHWs are effective primarily because they share language, culture, and lived experience with the patients they serve — building trust that clinical staff often cannot achieve, regardless of their clinical skill.

options.text: They have more clinical training than nurses or medical assistants
They share language, culture, and lived experience, enabling trust that clinical staff often cannot build
They can access patient records that clinical staff cannot
They work in community settings where patients feel less anxiety than in clinical settings

lessons.title: Cross-Sector Partnerships: Health Systems & Community Organizations
lessons.summary: How health systems, community organizations, housing agencies, schools, and food systems are building partnerships to address upstream determinants of health at scale.

objectives.text: Describe the 'anchor institution' role for health systems in community health
Explain IRS community benefit requirements for nonprofit hospitals
Identify examples of successful cross-sector partnerships and their outcomes

contentBlocks.heading: Hospitals as anchor institutions
contentBlocks.body:
Large health systems are often among the biggest employers in their communities — with massive purchasing power, real estate holdings, and investment portfolios. The 'anchor institution' concept asks: can health systems use these economic levers to benefit their communities, not just their patients?

Examples: Kaiser Permanente has committed $200M to affordable housing. Boston Medical Center runs a food pantry, farm, and kitchen that produces medically tailored meals. Cleveland Clinic's Evergreen Cooperative uses procurement to create jobs in underserved neighborhoods. These are not charity — they are strategic investments in the social determinants of health that drive the system's highest-cost patients.

contentBlocks.heading: Mechanisms for health system community investment

items.title: Procurement
items.body: Directing purchasing toward local, minority-owned businesses. Creates jobs and local economic circulation in high-need communities.

items.title: Investment
items.body: Mission-aligned investing in affordable housing, community development financial institutions (CDFIs), and social enterprises.

items.title: Workforce pipeline
items.body: Partnering with local schools and community colleges to create health career pathways for residents of communities the system serves.

items.title: Community health needs
items.body: IRS Section 501(r) requires nonprofit hospitals to conduct a Community Health Needs Assessment every 3 years and develop an implementation strategy. A mechanism for structured community investment.

contentBlocks.heading: Community benefit: $129B annually — but poorly tracked
contentBlocks.body: Nonprofit hospitals claimed $129B in community benefit spending in 2019 — mostly charity care and Medicaid shortfall. Critics argue that little of this reaches the social determinants investments that would most reduce community health disparities. The IRS requires community benefit reporting but allows wide flexibility in what counts. CMS and advocacy groups are pushing for requirements that a meaningful share of community benefit target measurable social determinants.

questions.question: What is the IRS Section 501(r) requirement for nonprofit hospitals related to community health?
questions.explanation: Section 501(r) requires nonprofit hospitals to conduct a Community Health Needs Assessment every 3 years and develop an implementation strategy addressing identified needs — as a condition of their tax-exempt status.

options.text: Nonprofit hospitals must spend at least 10% of revenue on charity care
Nonprofit hospitals must conduct a Community Health Needs Assessment every 3 years
Nonprofit hospitals must partner with at least one community health center
Nonprofit hospitals must report patient race and ethnicity data to CMS

lessons.title: Organizational Equity Transformation: From Policy to Culture
lessons.summary: What it takes to move health equity from a strategic initiative to an organizational culture — governance, leadership accountability, staff training, and the long arc of institutional change.

objectives.text: Identify the governance structures that support health equity transformation
Explain what 'equity-centered leadership' means in practice
Describe why training alone is insufficient for organizational equity change

contentBlocks.heading: Training is not transformation
contentBlocks.body:
Many health systems have invested in implicit bias training, diversity workshops, and equity awareness programs. These have value — but research consistently shows that training alone does not change organizational behavior or patient outcomes. Systems that achieve meaningful equity improvement do so through structural change: governance accountability, resource allocation, process redesign, and data-driven feedback loops.

The most effective equity transformations combine awareness (helping staff understand the problem) with structural change (redesigning processes so equitable outcomes are the default, not the exception).

items.title: Governance
items.body: Board-level equity committee with authority and budget. Board receives stratified quality and access data regularly. Equity metrics in CEO and senior leader scorecards.

items.title: Data accountability
items.body: Publicly reported equity metrics. Department-level disparity dashboards. Leaders see their unit's equity data alongside financial and clinical quality data.

items.title: Resource allocation
items.body: Dedicated equity improvement budget. Resources directed disproportionately toward identified gap areas. Community benefit investments tied to CHNA priorities.

items.title: Workforce diversity
items.body: Hiring practices, retention programs, and leadership development for staff from underrepresented communities. Representative workforce at every level, not just entry-level.

questions.question: What does research show about the effectiveness of implicit bias training alone as an equity intervention?
questions.explanation: Research consistently shows that training alone does not change organizational behavior or patient outcomes. Structural changes — governance accountability, process redesign, data feedback — are required for measurable improvement.

options.text: Implicit bias training alone consistently reduces racial disparities in care within 6 months
Training alone does not change behavior or outcomes — structural changes are required
Training is effective if delivered annually but loses effectiveness when done more frequently
Training effectiveness depends primarily on whether it is delivered by an internal or external trainer

title: AI & Machine Learning in Healthcare
subtitle: Predictive analytics, clinical decision support, LLMs, FDA regulation, algorithmic bias, and responsible implementation
description: A practical, rigorous introduction to artificial intelligence and machine learning in healthcare. Covers the fundamentals of ML, predictive analytics in clinical settings, natural language processing and LLMs in clinical notes, clinical decision support systems, FDA regulation of AI/ML-based devices, algorithmic bias, and a framework for responsible implementation. Designed for health professionals who need to evaluate, deploy, and govern AI tools — not just use them.
targetAudience: Clinical informatics and digital health staff
Health IT and data science staff
Physicians and nurses encountering AI at the bedside

tracks.title: AI & ML Fundamentals for Clinicians
tracks.description: The core concepts of machine learning — supervised, unsupervised, deep learning — explained for healthcare professionals without a data science background.

lessons.title: How Machine Learning Works: A Non-Technical Primer
lessons.summary: The difference between AI, ML, and deep learning; how supervised learning works; what training data is; and why 'the algorithm learned it' is not a sufficient explanation.

objectives.text: Explain the difference between AI, machine learning, and deep learning
Describe how supervised learning works at a conceptual level
Explain what training data is and why its quality determines model quality

contentBlocks.heading: AI is a broad term — here's how to navigate it
contentBlocks.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) refers broadly to machines performing tasks that would typically require human intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is a subset of AI: instead of being explicitly programmed with rules, ML systems learn patterns from data. Deep learning is a subset of ML that uses neural networks with many layers — it powers the most impressive recent advances in image recognition, language understanding, and clinical prediction.

In health care, when someone says 'AI,' they usually mean one of three things: a predictive model (will this patient be readmitted?), a computer vision tool (does this chest X-ray show pneumonia?), or a language model (summarize this clinical note).

items.title: Supervised learning
items.body: The model learns from labeled examples — inputs paired with correct outputs. Train on 10,000 labeled chest X-rays; the model learns to classify new ones. Most clinical AI is supervised.

items.title: Unsupervised learning
items.body: The model finds patterns in unlabeled data — clustering similar patients together, detecting anomalies. Used in patient stratification and cohort discovery.

items.title: Reinforcement learning
items.body: The model learns by trial and error, receiving rewards for good decisions. Used in robotic surgery, treatment protocol optimization, and dosing algorithms.

contentBlocks.heading: Training data: the model's foundation
contentBlocks.body:
A supervised learning model is only as good as its training data. The model learns the relationship between inputs (e.g., lab values, vital signs, demographics) and outputs (e.g., sepsis in next 6 hours: yes/no) from historical examples.

If the training data reflects historical biases — for example, if underdiagnosis of a condition in Black patients means fewer true positives in the training set — the model will learn those biases. If training data comes from one hospital system, the model may not generalize to different patient populations, clinical workflows, or EHR documentation styles.

This is why 'the algorithm was trained on millions of records' is not sufficient assurance of quality — the question is what was in those records.

contentBlocks.heading: Correlation is not causation — and AI doesn't know the difference
contentBlocks.body: ML models find statistical patterns. They have no understanding of mechanism, no concept of causality, and no ability to reason about novel situations. A model trained to predict sepsis might learn that low blood pressure correlates with sepsis — but it might also learn that certain nursing documentation patterns correlate, because nurses document more thoroughly for sicker patients. Both patterns predict sepsis, but only one is clinically meaningful. This is why human oversight remains essential.

contentBlocks.caption: Machine learning in medicine — MIT overview (~10 min)

questions.question: A hospital trains a sepsis prediction model on 5 years of its own EHR data. Which of the following is the strongest concern about deploying this model at a different hospital?
questions.explanation: Models trained on one institution's data may not generalize to others due to differences in patient populations, documentation practices, and clinical workflows — a problem called distribution shift.

options.text: The model will be too expensive to license from the original hospital
The model may not generalize due to differences in patient populations and documentation practices
The model requires the same EHR vendor as the training institution
The model will predict outcomes that were only relevant 5 years ago

questions.question: What is 'supervised learning'?

options.text: Learning that requires a human supervisor to approve each model prediction
Learning from labeled examples — inputs paired with correct outputs
Learning performed under regulatory supervision by the FDA
Learning from unlabeled data to find hidden patterns

lessons.title: Reading AI Performance Metrics: Sensitivity, Specificity & AUC
lessons.summary: The performance metrics used to evaluate clinical AI — sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, AUC-ROC — and why the right metric depends on the clinical use case.

objectives.text: Define sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV in clinical AI context
Explain the sensitivity-specificity tradeoff and when each matters more
Interpret an AUC-ROC score and its limitations

contentBlocks.heading: Why '95% accurate' tells you almost nothing
contentBlocks.body: A vendor claims their sepsis model is '95% accurate.' What does that mean? If only 5% of patients get sepsis, a model that always predicts 'no sepsis' achieves 95% accuracy — while being completely useless. Accuracy alone is meaningless. Clinical AI must be evaluated on metrics that reflect the cost of errors in the specific clinical context.

contentBlocks.heading: The core performance metrics
contentBlocks.rightLabel: What it measures / When it matters most

rows.label: Sensitivity (recall)
rows.right: When missing a case is dangerous — sepsis, cancer screening. High sensitivity = few false negatives.

rows.label: Specificity
rows.right: When false alarms cause harm — alert fatigue, unnecessary procedures. High specificity = few false positives.

rows.label: PPV (precision)
rows.left: % of positive predictions that are actually positive
rows.right: How actionable is a positive alert? Depends heavily on prevalence.

rows.label: NPV
rows.left: % of negative predictions that are actually negative
rows.right: How confident can you be when the model says no disease?

rows.label: AUC-ROC
rows.left: Overall discriminative ability across all thresholds
rows.right: Useful for comparing models; insensitive to class imbalance. Values: 0.5 = chance; 0.9+ = excellent.

contentBlocks.heading: Prevalence changes everything
contentBlocks.body: A test with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity sounds excellent. But in a population where only 1% have the disease (low prevalence), the PPV is only about 8% — meaning 92% of positive results are false alarms. The same test in a high-risk population (20% prevalence) has PPV ~70%. Always ask: what is the base rate of the condition this model predicts in my patient population?

questions.question: A sepsis prediction model has high sensitivity but low specificity. What is the primary clinical risk of deploying it?
questions.explanation: Low specificity means many false positives — many patients flagged as having sepsis who don't. In practice, this causes alert fatigue: clinicians start ignoring alerts because most are wrong.

options.text: Many sepsis cases will be missed
Alert fatigue — too many false alarms causing clinicians to ignore alerts
The model will perform poorly on non-sepsis diagnoses
The model will be biased against elderly patients

lessons.title: Deep Learning in Medical Imaging: Radiology, Pathology & Ophthalmology
lessons.summary: How convolutional neural networks work in medical imaging, the landmark studies in radiology and pathology AI, and the evidence on diagnostic accuracy vs. clinicians.

objectives.text: Explain how convolutional neural networks process medical images
Describe landmark imaging AI studies in radiology, pathology, and ophthalmology
Evaluate AI vs. clinician accuracy claims critically

contentBlocks.heading: Why images are where AI excels
contentBlocks.body:
Medical images — X-rays, CT scans, pathology slides, fundus photographs — are where deep learning has demonstrated the most striking clinical results. Unlike structured data (labs, vitals) that requires feature engineering, images can be fed directly into convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which learn to extract relevant features automatically.

The CNN's core operation: filters scan across the image at multiple scales, detecting edges, textures, and shapes at increasing levels of abstraction. Early layers detect simple features (lines, blobs); deeper layers detect complex patterns (the irregular border of a malignant mass, the drusen deposits of diabetic macular edema).

contentBlocks.heading: Landmark imaging AI results by specialty

items.title: Chest X-ray (radiology)
items.body: CheXNet (Stanford 2017): CNN diagnosed 14 chest conditions from chest X-rays at or above radiologist accuracy. Followed by Google's study of chest X-rays for tuberculosis in low-resource settings.

items.title: Diabetic retinopathy
items.body: Google (2016): CNN detected diabetic retinopathy from fundus photos at or above ophthalmologist level, with ~90% sensitivity/specificity. FDA cleared for autonomous use — no ophthalmologist required.

items.title: Pathology (cancer)
items.body: Google and Memorial Sloan Kettering: CNNs detect breast cancer metastases in lymph node slides at higher accuracy than pathologists. Also strong results in prostate, colon, and lung cancer.

items.title: Cardiac imaging
items.body: EchoNet (Stanford): CNN estimates ejection fraction from echocardiograms with cardiologist-level accuracy. Enables automated screening of cardiac function at scale.

contentBlocks.heading: AI vs. clinician comparisons: read the fine print
contentBlocks.body: Headlines announcing 'AI outperforms doctors' require careful reading. Key questions: (1) What is the AI compared to — a single radiologist, or a consensus of specialists? (2) Was the test set independent, or from the same institution as training? (3) Was the AI deployed in real workflow, or evaluated on curated images? (4) What happened to performance on subgroups? Studies that show AI matching single clinicians on curated test sets often show degraded performance in real-world deployment.

questions.question: What is the most important question to ask when a study claims an imaging AI 'outperforms' clinicians?
