questions.explanation: The comparison group matters enormously. AI may outperform a single junior clinician but not a panel of subspecialists. The test dataset quality, independence from training data, and real-world validation all determine whether the claim is meaningful.

options.text: What hardware was used to run the AI model?
Who was the AI compared to, and was the test set independent from training data?
What journal published the study?
What was the sample size of the training dataset?

tracks.title: Predictive Analytics in Clinical Practice
tracks.description: Readmission prediction, sepsis early warning, deterioration models, and the evidence on whether these tools actually improve outcomes.

lessons.title: Readmission Prediction: The LACE Score, ML Models & What the Evidence Shows
lessons.summary: The history and evidence on 30-day readmission prediction, from the LACE index to ML models, and the honest answer about whether prediction actually reduces readmissions.

objectives.text: Describe how readmission prediction models work and what inputs they use
Summarize the evidence on whether ML readmission models outperform simpler tools
Explain the gap between prediction accuracy and intervention effectiveness

contentBlocks.heading: The readmission problem and the HRRP
contentBlocks.body:
Hospital readmissions within 30 days are costly ($26B/year in Medicare) and often preventable. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), created by the ACA, penalizes hospitals with above-expected readmission rates for heart failure, pneumonia, hip/knee replacement, CABG, COPD, and MI. This created a strong financial incentive to identify and intervene with high-risk patients before discharge.

Readmission prediction was one of the first widespread applications of ML in clinical care. The LACE index (Length of stay, Acuity of admission, Charlson Comorbidity Index score, Emergency visits in past 6 months) was an early validated tool. ML models came later, promising to improve accuracy.

contentBlocks.heading: The prediction-intervention gap
contentBlocks.body: A landmark 2019 JAMA study found that despite being an excellent predictor of readmission, a widely deployed ML model from a major EHR vendor did not improve patient outcomes — because hospitals lacked effective interventions to deploy after a high-risk alert. Prediction without effective intervention is just an expensive alert system. The hard problem is not prediction; it's what you do after.

contentBlocks.heading: What high-performing readmission programs actually do
contentBlocks.body: The hospitals that have most reduced readmissions are not the ones with the best prediction models. They are the ones with: dedicated transition care nurses who call patients within 48 hours of discharge, partnerships with home health agencies, pharmacists who reconcile medications, and post-discharge clinic slots. Prediction identifies who needs those services — but the services must actually exist.

questions.question: What does the 'prediction-intervention gap' mean in the context of readmission prediction?
questions.explanation: Even accurate prediction models don't reduce readmissions unless there are effective interventions available to deploy for high-risk patients — a problem consistently found in readmission research.

options.text: Prediction models work better for some diagnoses than others
Accurate prediction does not reduce readmissions unless effective interventions are available and deployed
Predictions made at admission are less accurate than those made at discharge
ML models predict better than simpler tools but are harder to implement

lessons.title: Sepsis Early Warning Systems: Evidence & Alert Fatigue
lessons.summary: The landscape of sepsis prediction tools (Epic Sepsis Model, SOFA, qSOFA), the landmark Johns Hopkins study exposing the Epic model, and the alert fatigue problem.

objectives.text: Describe the Epic Sepsis Model and the Johns Hopkins JAMA study findings
Explain what alert fatigue is and its consequences for patient safety
Identify design principles that reduce alert fatigue

contentBlocks.heading: Sepsis prediction at scale
contentBlocks.body:
Sepsis — dysregulated host response to infection leading to life-threatening organ dysfunction — is one of the most time-sensitive conditions in medicine. An hour's delay in treatment increases mortality. This makes it an attractive target for AI early warning.

Epic Systems, the dominant EHR vendor, built a proprietary Sepsis Model (ESM) into its system, deployed at hundreds of hospitals. Clinicians receive alerts when a patient's ESM score exceeds a threshold.

contentBlocks.heading: The Johns Hopkins finding
contentBlocks.body: A 2021 JAMA Internal Medicine study from Johns Hopkins evaluated the Epic Sepsis Model prospectively in their system. Results: the model had poor sensitivity (63%) and poor specificity — for every true sepsis case flagged, there were many false alarms. The model missed 1 in 3 sepsis cases and generated so many false alerts that clinicians learned to discount them. The study concluded the ESM performed no better than simpler clinical scoring tools and contributed to alert fatigue.

items.title: What it is
items.body: When clinicians receive so many alerts — mostly false or non-actionable — that they begin ignoring or overriding them routinely.

items.title: Scale
items.body: Studies show 50–90% of clinical alerts are overridden or ignored. Physicians receive 63–100+ alerts per day in high-acuity settings.

items.title: Safety risk
items.body: When real critical alerts are buried among dozens of false ones, clinicians may miss the one that matters. Alert fatigue has been linked to preventable patient harm.

items.title: Solutions
items.body: Alert optimization: reduce alert volume by raising thresholds, removing low-value alerts, adding specificity to triggers, and presenting alerts with actionable options.

questions.question: What did the 2021 Johns Hopkins JAMA study find about the Epic Sepsis Model?
questions.explanation: The study found the Epic Sepsis Model had poor sensitivity (missing 1 in 3 sepsis cases), generated many false positives, contributed to alert fatigue, and performed no better than simpler clinical scoring tools.

options.text: The model successfully reduced sepsis mortality at Johns Hopkins by 20%
The model had poor sensitivity and specificity, contributed to alert fatigue, and performed no better than simpler tools
The model worked well for ICU patients but poorly for ward patients
Epic's model was found to be biased against elderly patients

lessons.title: Inpatient Deterioration Models: NEWS, eCART & Real-Time ML
lessons.summary: How clinical deterioration is detected in inpatient settings — from traditional vital sign scoring (NEWS, MEWS) to ML-based deterioration models — and the alert fatigue tradeoffs.

objectives.text: Describe traditional early warning scores (NEWS, MEWS) and how they are calculated
Explain how ML-based deterioration models differ from rule-based scoring
Describe the evidence on ML deterioration models' clinical impact

contentBlocks.heading: The clinical deterioration problem
contentBlocks.body:
Approximately 200,000 hospital patients experience preventable in-hospital cardiac arrest annually in the US. Many of these events are preceded by hours of physiologic deterioration that is visible in vital signs and other clinical data — if someone is looking. Early warning systems aim to detect that deterioration before irreversible harm occurs.

Traditional early warning scores (NEWS, MEWS, CURB-65) use simple point systems: add points for abnormal vital signs, reach a threshold, trigger an alert or rapid response. They are transparent and easy to explain, but static — they can't learn from your specific institution's patient population or outcome patterns.

contentBlocks.heading: Traditional scores vs. ML deterioration models

rows.label: Input data
rows.right: Vitals + labs + medications + notes + nursing documentation

rows.label: Learning
rows.right: Trained on institutional data, can be retrained

rows.label: Transparency
rows.left: Fully explainable — clinicians understand the score
rows.right: Black box — clinicians may not understand why alert fired

rows.label: Performance
rows.right: AUC ~0.85–0.90 in training/validation studies

rows.label: Real-world impact
rows.left: Mixed — rapid response teams reduce arrest rates when systems are well-designed
rows.right: Limited RCT evidence; some studies show alert fatigue outweighs benefit

contentBlocks.heading: eCART: the best-studied ML deterioration model
contentBlocks.body: The electronic Cardiac Arrest Risk Triage (eCART) model, developed at the University of Chicago, uses 30+ variables from the EHR to predict cardiac arrest and ICU transfer within 24 hours. Prospective studies show AUC 0.86 — substantially better than NEWS alone. But real-world deployment studies found that alert frequency determined clinical impact: sites that fired alerts too frequently saw alert fatigue; those with carefully calibrated thresholds saw RRT activation improvements.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of ML-based deterioration models over traditional early warning scores like NEWS?
questions.explanation: ML models can incorporate many more input variables — labs, medications, nursing documentation — and learn from institutional data, achieving higher discriminative accuracy than simple vital sign scoring systems.

options.text: They are more transparent and easier for bedside nurses to understand
They incorporate more data types and learn from institutional patterns, achieving higher AUC
They require less IT infrastructure to deploy than rule-based systems
They have been proven to reduce mortality in RCTs across multiple hospital systems

lessons.title: AI for Population Health: Risk Stratification & Care Gap Identification
lessons.summary: How analytics platforms use ML to stratify patient populations, identify rising-risk patients before crisis, and target care management resources efficiently.

objectives.text: Explain how risk stratification models identify rising-risk patients
Describe the difference between retrospective and prospective risk models
Identify the major population health analytics platforms and their approaches

contentBlocks.heading: The population health challenge
contentBlocks.body:
ACOs and value-based care organizations are accountable for the total cost of care for attributed populations — often 10,000–100,000 patients. They cannot intensively manage every patient; resources are finite. The goal of population health analytics is to identify which patients need what intensity of care management, and to deliver the right intervention at the right time.

Risk stratification models classify patients by predicted future cost and utilization: high risk (top 1–5%, very high expected cost), rising risk (next 10–15%, trending toward high cost and most actionable), and low risk (stable, managed through primary care). The rising-risk segment is the highest-value target for proactive intervention.

items.title: Future cost
items.body: Predict which patients will generate the highest total spend in the next 12 months. Used to allocate care management resources and identify members for outreach.

items.title: Hospitalization risk
items.body: Predict likelihood of hospitalization or ED visit in the next 30–90 days. Enables proactive outreach before the crisis event.

items.title: Care gap identification
items.body: Identify patients overdue for preventive services (colonoscopy, mammogram, A1c, blood pressure check). Enables targeted outreach to improve quality measure rates.

items.title: Adherence risk
items.body: Predict which patients are likely to be non-adherent to medications based on pharmacy fill data, prior patterns, and social factors.

contentBlocks.heading: Actionability over accuracy
contentBlocks.body: The most predictive population health model is not always the most useful. A model that accurately predicts the highest-cost 1% of patients (who have advanced cancer, ESRD on dialysis, or end-stage HF) may identify patients for whom intensive care management can't change the trajectory. High-performing ACOs focus on the 'rising risk' segment — patients who are trending toward high cost but are still early enough to benefit from intervention. Actionability, not raw predictive accuracy, is the right optimization target.

questions.question: Why do high-performing ACOs often focus care management resources on 'rising-risk' patients rather than the highest-risk tier?
questions.explanation: The highest-risk patients (advanced terminal illness, end-stage disease) often cannot benefit from care management intervention. Rising-risk patients are still in a window where proactive intervention can change trajectory — making them the highest-value target.

options.text: Rising-risk patients are less expensive to manage per case
Rising-risk patients are still in a window where proactive intervention can change trajectory
CMS requires ACOs to focus on rising-risk patients under MSSP rules
Highest-risk patients prefer not to be enrolled in care management programs

tracks.title: NLP & LLMs in Clinical Care
tracks.description: How natural language processing works in clinical contexts, the rise of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare, and the evidence and risks of ambient clinical documentation.

lessons.title: LLMs in Healthcare: Ambient Documentation, Summarization & Hallucination
lessons.summary: How LLMs (like GPT-4 and clinical variants) are being used for ambient documentation, clinical note summarization, patient messaging, and the critical risk of hallucination.

objectives.text: Explain what large language models are and how they generate text
Describe the clinical use cases for LLMs and their evidence base
Explain what hallucination is and why it is a patient safety issue in clinical LLM applications

contentBlocks.heading: LLMs: pattern completion at massive scale
contentBlocks.body:
Large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Claude, and their clinical variants (Med-PaLM, NYUTron) are trained on vast corpora of text to predict the next token in a sequence. They are not retrieving facts from a database — they are generating statistically likely continuations of text.

This makes them remarkably capable at tasks that look like language understanding: summarizing text, drafting responses, extracting information from notes, answering questions. It also makes them capable of generating plausible-sounding but false content — a phenomenon called hallucination.

contentBlocks.heading: Clinical LLM use cases (with evidence status)

items.title: Ambient documentation
items.body: LLM listens to clinical encounter, generates draft SOAP note. Evidence: 70%+ of physicians report time savings. Risk: hallucination of clinical details not spoken.

items.title: Discharge summary
items.body: Summarize hospital course from structured and unstructured EHR data. Promising for reducing documentation burden. Requires robust validation workflow.

items.title: Patient message drafting
items.body: LLM drafts responses to patient portal messages for physician review. Early evidence: reduces response time, physician-reviewed before sending reduces risk.

items.title: Chart review / abstraction
items.body: Extract clinical data from unstructured notes at scale — for quality reporting, research, or pre-authorization. Risk: misextraction in dense clinical text.

contentBlocks.heading: Hallucination: the clinical safety issue
contentBlocks.body:
LLMs hallucinate — they generate confident-sounding text that is factually false. In an ambient documentation context: a physician discusses a patient's medication list but the LLM generates a drug dose that was never stated. In a discharge summary: the LLM includes a diagnosis that was considered but ruled out. In a Q&A context: the LLM cites a clinical guideline that doesn't exist.

Hallucination rates vary by task and model but are never zero. Every clinical LLM deployment must have: (1) a clinician review step before information enters the clinical record, (2) clear disclosure to patients that AI was involved, and (3) monitoring for hallucination rates in production.

contentBlocks.label: Physician using ambient documentation: real-world experience
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a physician who has been using an AI ambient documentation tool (like Nuance DAX, Abridge, or similar) for at least 3 months — what works, what doesn't, what they've had to correct, and how it has changed their workflow. Recommended: 8–10 minutes.

questions.question: What is 'hallucination' in the context of large language models?
questions.explanation: Hallucination refers to LLMs generating confident-sounding text that is factually false — not due to intentional deception, but because LLMs generate statistically probable text rather than retrieving verified facts.

options.text: When the LLM generates text that is politically biased
When the LLM generates confident-sounding but factually false content
When the LLM fails to understand medical terminology
When the LLM produces text that plagiarizes clinical guidelines

lessons.title: NLP for Clinical Notes: Information Extraction & Coding
lessons.summary: How traditional NLP (before LLMs) works on clinical text — named entity recognition, relation extraction, ICD coding automation, and the uses in quality measurement and research.

objectives.text: Explain named entity recognition (NER) and its application to clinical notes
Describe how NLP is used for automated ICD coding and quality measure abstraction
Compare traditional NLP approaches to LLM-based approaches for clinical text

contentBlocks.heading: The unstructured data problem
contentBlocks.body:
80% of clinical data lives in unstructured text — physician notes, nursing documentation, radiology reports, discharge summaries. Structured data (diagnoses, labs, medications) captures what the EHR was designed to capture; notes capture the nuance, context, reasoning, and clinical judgment that structured fields cannot.

Traditional NLP approaches extract structured information from this text using statistical models trained to recognize entities (diseases, medications, symptoms) and their relationships (drug X treats condition Y; finding Z is not present). These approaches are faster, more predictable, and more auditable than LLMs for high-stakes extraction tasks.

items.title: Named entity recognition
items.body: Identifying clinical concepts in text: 'The patient has type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3.' NER extracts and normalizes these to standard codes.

items.title: ICD-10 coding
items.body: Automated coding from clinical notes. Reduces coder burden, improves consistency. AI-assisted coding (not fully automated) is increasingly standard in large health systems.

items.title: Quality measure abstraction
items.body: Extracting quality measure data from notes at scale — identifying smoking status, BMI, depression screening results, advance directive documentation.

items.title: Adverse event detection
items.body: Scanning notes for safety signals — fall mentions, medication errors, hospital-acquired conditions — at population scale for patient safety surveillance.

contentBlocks.heading: Traditional NLP vs. LLMs for clinical text

rows.label: Speed
rows.left: Fast — can process millions of notes
rows.right: Slower — expensive at scale

rows.label: Consistency
rows.left: Highly consistent — same input → same output
rows.right: Can vary across runs (temperature > 0)

rows.label: Transparency
rows.left: More auditable for specific extraction tasks
rows.right: Less auditable — harder to trace why output was generated

rows.label: Flexibility
rows.right: Flexible — can handle novel tasks with prompting

rows.label: Hallucination
rows.right: Can generate plausible but false extractions

questions.question: For high-volume, high-stakes clinical text extraction (like automated ICD coding), why might traditional NLP models be preferred over LLMs?
questions.explanation: Traditional NLP is faster, more consistent, more auditable, and less prone to hallucination than LLMs for structured extraction tasks — important qualities for high-stakes, high-volume applications like coding.

options.text: Traditional NLP is always more accurate than LLMs on clinical text
Traditional NLP is faster, more consistent, and less likely to fabricate content
LLMs cannot process clinical notes — they only work on consumer language
Traditional NLP is cheaper to develop but not to run at scale

tracks.title: Clinical Decision Support
tracks.description: The landscape of clinical decision support systems (CDSS), the difference between rule-based and ML-based CDS, the 21st Century Cures Act CDS provisions, and evidence on CDSS effectiveness.

lessons.title: Clinical Decision Support: From Drug Alerts to ML-Powered Recommendations
lessons.summary: The spectrum of CDSS from simple drug-drug interaction alerts to ML-powered diagnostic support, what works, what doesn't, and the 21st Century Cures Act's CDS provisions.

objectives.text: Describe the spectrum of CDSS from rule-based to ML-powered
Identify CDSS types with the strongest evidence for improving outcomes
Explain the 21st Century Cures Act's treatment of clinical decision support software

contentBlocks.heading: CDS has been in EHRs for decades
contentBlocks.body:
Clinical decision support is not new. Drug-drug interaction alerts, allergy warnings, dosing calculators, and order sets are all forms of CDS that have been in EHRs since the 1990s. The problem: most of them are wrong most of the time — not because the underlying clinical logic is wrong, but because alert thresholds are set too low, generating constant warnings for interactions that are rarely clinically significant.

The result is the same as with sepsis alerts: clinicians learn to click through. Studies show physicians override 90%+ of drug-drug interaction alerts. The signal is lost in noise.

rows.label: How it works
rows.left: If-then logic written by humans (e.g., 'if penicillin allergy + amoxicillin order → alert')
rows.right: Statistical model trained on data finds patterns and makes recommendations

rows.label: Transparency
rows.right: Often a 'black box' — model internals may not be interpretable

rows.label: Adaptability
rows.right: Can be retrained as new data arrives

rows.label: Use cases
rows.left: Drug interactions, dosing, contraindications, preventive care reminders
rows.right: Sepsis prediction, deterioration alerts, diagnostic support, care gap identification

rows.label: Evidence
rows.left: Strong for some (dosing, preventive care); poor for others (drug interaction alerts)
rows.right: Mixed — some tools improve outcomes; many fail to demonstrate benefit in practice

contentBlocks.heading: 21st Century Cures Act: CDS as a software device?
contentBlocks.body: The 21st Century Cures Act created a new regulatory category distinguishing 'clinical decision support software' that is FDA-regulated (Software as a Medical Device, or SaMD) from CDS that is not. Key distinction: CDS that requires clinician review and judgment before action is NOT a medical device (not FDA-regulated). CDS that acts autonomously or overrides clinician judgment may be regulated. This distinction is critical for understanding which AI tools require FDA clearance.

questions.question: Under the 21st Century Cures Act framework, when does clinical decision support software become a regulated medical device?
questions.explanation: CDS that requires clinician review and judgment is not regulated as a medical device. CDS that acts autonomously or overrides clinician judgment may be regulated as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD).

options.text: When it is used in an inpatient setting rather than outpatient
When it acts autonomously or overrides clinician judgment, rather than supporting it
When it is sold commercially, as opposed to built internally by a health system
When it uses ML rather than rule-based logic

lessons.title: CDS That Works: Evidence-Based Design Principles
lessons.summary: What the evidence shows about which CDSS features improve outcomes — the 'five rights' of CDS, the importance of workflow integration, and why override rates matter.

objectives.text: Apply the 'five rights' of CDS to evaluate a clinical alert design
Explain the importance of workflow integration in CDS effectiveness
Describe what alert override rates reveal about CDS quality

contentBlocks.heading: The five rights of clinical decision support
contentBlocks.body:
The Office of the National Coordinator's Health IT Policy Committee developed the 'Five Rights' framework for effective CDS: the right information, to the right person, in the right format, through the right channel, at the right time.

This framework captures why most clinical alerts fail: they deliver the right information (technically correct clinical logic) to the wrong person (the ordering physician, not the pharmacist who should review it), in the wrong format (disruptive modal alert instead of a background recommendation), through the wrong channel (EHR, when the workflow is verbal), at the wrong time (after the order is entered instead of during ordering).

contentBlocks.heading: The Five Rights of CDS applied

items.title: Right information
items.body: Evidence-based, clinically current. Alert content must be maintained as evidence evolves — outdated CDS is worse than no CDS.

items.title: Right person
items.body: Who can act on this information? A drug interaction alert firing for a nurse who cannot change an order without physician approval wastes attention.

items.title: Right format
items.body: Passive suggestion (infobutton), active notification, or hard stop? Match the level of interruption to the severity and urgency of the issue.

items.title: Right channel
items.body: In-workflow (at time of ordering), at-a-glance (dashboard), or asynchronous (inbox message). Channel choice determines whether the CDS is seen and actionable.

items.title: Right time
items.body: CDS fired before an order is finalized is 10x more effective than the same alert firing after the order is submitted. Timing determines whether the clinician can still act.

contentBlocks.heading: Override rates: what they tell you
contentBlocks.body: A CDS alert with a 90% override rate is almost certainly misconfigured. Clinicians override alerts when they are wrong (false positives), irrelevant (doesn't apply to this patient's situation), or trust-eroding (have been overriding alerts for years). Rather than accepting override rates as a proxy for poor physician compliance, treat high override rates as a signal that the alert design needs to be fixed. The goal is alerts with 40–70% action rates — fired less frequently, but on cases that warrant action.

questions.question: According to the 'Five Rights' of CDS, which factor is most important for maximizing alert action rates?
questions.explanation: Timing is among the most critical — CDS delivered at the point of ordering (before the order is finalized) is far more likely to change behavior than the same alert delivered after the order is placed, when changing it requires additional steps.

options.text: The technical accuracy of the clinical evidence underlying the alert
Delivering the alert at the right time — before the order is finalized rather than after
The visual design of the alert modal window
Whether the alert is approved by the medical informatics committee

tracks.title: FDA Regulation of AI/ML in Healthcare
tracks.description: How the FDA regulates AI/ML-based medical devices, the SaMD framework, predicate devices, and the challenge of regulating continuously learning algorithms.
targetAudience: Medical device and digital health staff

lessons.title: FDA & AI: SaMD, 510(k), and the Regulation of Learning Algorithms
lessons.summary: How the FDA classifies and reviews AI/ML-based software as medical devices, the 510(k) pathway, De Novo classification, and the evolving framework for AI that continuously learns.

objectives.text: Explain what Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) is and when FDA regulation applies
Describe the 510(k) and De Novo pathways for AI/ML medical devices
Explain the unique regulatory challenge posed by continuously learning AI algorithms

contentBlocks.heading: When is AI a medical device?
contentBlocks.body:
The FDA regulates software that meets the definition of a medical device: intended for use in diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease, or to affect the structure or function of the body.

Software that performs these functions is called Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). An AI algorithm that analyzes a chest X-ray and outputs 'no pneumonia detected' or 'possible malignancy — clinical review recommended' is a medical device. The software that schedules appointments or encrypts data is not.

As of 2024, the FDA has cleared or approved over 700 AI/ML-based medical devices — the vast majority in radiology, cardiology, and ophthalmology.

stats.label: AI/ML-based medical devices cleared or approved by FDA (through 2024)
Of cleared AI devices are in radiology
Most common review pathway — requires showing substantial equivalence to a predicate device
Year FDA released its action plan for AI/ML-based SaMD

contentBlocks.heading: The continuously learning algorithm problem
contentBlocks.body:
Traditional medical devices are static — they don't change after approval. AI algorithms can be designed to continuously learn from new data, which means the algorithm you approve today may be different from the algorithm deployed a year later.

FDA's current framework (Predetermined Change Control Plan) requires manufacturers to pre-specify what kinds of changes the algorithm may make to itself, and what monitoring will ensure it remains safe and effective. This is an evolving regulatory area — the rules are being written as technology advances.

contentBlocks.heading: FDA review pathways for AI devices

items.title: 510(k) Clearance
items.body: Most AI devices use this path. Manufacturer shows 'substantial equivalence' to a legally marketed predicate device. Risk-based — Class II devices.

items.title: De Novo
items.body: For novel low-to-moderate risk devices with no predicate. Creates new classification and can become a predicate for future 510(k)s.

items.title: PMA (Premarket Approval)
items.body: Highest scrutiny. Required for Class III (highest risk) devices. Rare for AI — most AI tools are Class II.

items.title: PCCP
items.body: Predetermined Change Control Plan — manufacturer pre-specifies algorithm change types; FDA approves plan upfront rather than reviewing each change.

questions.question: Why do continuously learning AI algorithms pose a unique regulatory challenge for the FDA?
questions.explanation: The FDA typically approves a fixed device. If an AI algorithm changes itself through ongoing learning, the approved version and the deployed version may diverge — requiring new frameworks like the PCCP to manage algorithm evolution safely.

options.text: They are too complex for FDA reviewers who lack ML expertise
The algorithm may change after approval, making the approved version different from what's deployed
They require more clinical trials than static algorithms
Continuously learning algorithms cannot be patented, creating IP challenges

lessons.title: FDA-Cleared AI Devices: Case Studies in Radiology & Cardiology
lessons.summary: Real-world case studies of FDA-cleared AI medical devices — chest X-ray triage tools, stroke detection, diabetic retinopathy screening — and what their market adoption reveals about real-world performance vs. regulatory claims.

objectives.text: Describe three FDA-cleared AI medical devices and their intended use
Explain the gap between FDA clearance and real-world evidence of clinical benefit
Identify questions health systems should ask when evaluating FDA-cleared AI tools

items.title: Viz.ai — Stroke AI
items.body: AI triage for CT scans showing large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke. Alerts stroke team simultaneously with CT read. FDA-cleared 2018. RCT evidence shows 37-minute faster time-to-treatment.

items.title: IDx-DR — Retinopathy
items.body: First FDA-authorized AI device requiring no specialist oversight (autonomous). Images diabetic patient's retina; returns 'more than mild diabetic retinopathy detected' or 'negative.' Primary care clinicians can deploy without ophthalmologist.

items.title: Aidoc — Chest CT triage
items.body: AI flags critical findings (PE, pneumothorax, aortic dissection) on chest CT for radiologist prioritization. FDA-cleared. Does not replace radiologist read — helps with worklist prioritization.

items.title: AliveCor — KardiaMobile
items.body: Consumer ECG device with FDA-cleared AI for atrial fibrillation detection. First AI-powered cardiac rhythm detection cleared for consumer use. 98% sensitivity for AFib.

contentBlocks.heading: FDA clearance ≠ evidence of clinical benefit
contentBlocks.body: Most AI devices reach FDA clearance through the 510(k) pathway, which requires demonstrating substantial equivalence to a predicate device — not clinical benefit. A device can be FDA-cleared without a single randomized controlled trial showing it improves patient outcomes. Health systems evaluating AI tools should ask: beyond FDA clearance, is there real-world evidence of clinical benefit in deployed settings similar to ours?

contentBlocks.heading: Post-market surveillance: the evidence gap
contentBlocks.body:
After FDA clearance, AI device performance is self-monitored by manufacturers with limited external oversight. CMS and FDA are developing Total Product Lifecycle (TPLC) surveillance frameworks — requiring manufacturers to monitor real-world performance continuously, report performance changes, and update their Predetermined Change Control Plans.

In the meantime, health systems are largely on their own in monitoring whether cleared devices are performing as expected in their patient populations. Many have found significant performance degradation when deploying AI tools trained on different populations — particularly for underrepresented racial and ethnic groups.

questions.question: What is significant about IDx-DR's FDA authorization compared to most other AI medical devices?
questions.explanation: IDx-DR was the first FDA-authorized AI device that can be used autonomously in primary care without requiring a specialist (ophthalmologist) to interpret results — a new regulatory category.

options.text: It was the first AI device to receive PMA approval rather than 510(k) clearance
It was the first FDA-authorized AI device authorized for autonomous use without specialist oversight
It was the first AI device covered by Medicare as a standalone service
It was trained on data from 50 countries, making it the most globally validated AI device

tracks.title: Bias, Fairness & Equity in Clinical AI
tracks.description: How AI systems encode and amplify health disparities, frameworks for bias evaluation, and what health systems can do to deploy AI equitably.

lessons.title: AI Fairness: Evaluation Frameworks & Equity by Design
lessons.summary: How to evaluate AI tools for bias before and after deployment, what 'fairness' means mathematically (and why different definitions conflict), and practical equity-by-design principles.

objectives.text: Describe at least three mathematical definitions of algorithmic fairness
Explain why different fairness definitions can be mathematically incompatible
Identify practical steps health systems can take to evaluate and monitor AI equity

contentBlocks.heading: Fairness is not one thing
contentBlocks.body:
When people say an AI system should be 'fair,' they often assume there is a clear definition. There is not. Researchers have identified more than 20 mathematical definitions of algorithmic fairness — and several are provably incompatible. You cannot simultaneously satisfy all of them.

This is not a reason for paralysis. It is a reason for being explicit about which definition of fairness you are optimizing for, and why — because the choice has consequences for different patient groups.

contentBlocks.heading: Three key fairness concepts (and their conflicts)

items.title: Demographic parity
items.body: The model should produce the same positive prediction rate across groups. Problem: if true prevalence differs by group, demographic parity requires the model to ignore real differences.

items.title: Equal opportunity
items.body: The model should have the same true positive rate (sensitivity) across groups — same recall for those with the condition. Prioritizes not missing cases in any group.

items.title: Calibration
items.body: When the model says 30% risk, 30% of patients in each group should actually have the outcome. Important for clinical use — calibration failure by group means predictions mean different things for different patients.

contentBlocks.heading: Practical equity evaluation for health systems
contentBlocks.body:
When evaluating an AI tool for procurement or deployment:
1. Ask the vendor for subgroup performance data — sensitivity, specificity, and calibration stratified by race, ethnicity, age, sex, and insurance status
2. Validate in your own patient population before deployment
3. Monitor performance continuously after deployment — AI models degrade over time and may degrade unevenly across groups
4. Create a process for clinicians to flag concerning model behavior

contentBlocks.label: Health system equity and AI: building governance
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a CMIO, CDO, or equity officer at a health system about how they evaluate AI tools for equity before procurement, what governance processes they use, and what they wish they had done differently with early deployments. Recommended: 8–12 minutes.

questions.question: Why should health systems ask for 'subgroup performance data' when evaluating an AI tool from a vendor?
questions.explanation: Aggregate performance metrics can hide poor performance in specific demographic subgroups. A model may work well overall but have significantly lower sensitivity for Black patients, older patients, or patients with different insurance — which would perpetuate disparities at scale.

options.text: To verify that the vendor collected data legally under HIPAA
Because aggregate metrics can hide poor performance in specific patient subgroups
To ensure the model was trained on data from their specific region
To determine whether the model requires FDA clearance

lessons.title: An Equity Framework for AI Procurement
lessons.summary: A practical toolkit for health systems: the questions to ask vendors, the internal assessments to run, and the governance processes that create accountability for AI equity.

objectives.text: Apply an equity assessment framework to a hypothetical AI vendor pitch
Identify what documentation health systems should require from AI vendors
Describe the internal governance processes that embed equity into AI decision-making

contentBlocks.heading: The equity assessment gap
contentBlocks.body:
A 2023 survey of health system AI governance programs found that fewer than 25% had a formal process for evaluating AI tools for equity before procurement. Most relied on vendor representations and FDA clearance as proxies for trustworthiness — neither of which addresses equity performance in the buying organization's specific patient population.

Building an equity assessment process is not optional for health systems that serve diverse or vulnerable populations under value-based contracts. Deploying a biased AI tool at scale can cause more harm than the problem it was designed to solve.

items.title: Training data
items.body: Ask: Where was the model trained? What was the demographic composition of the training population? Was race/ethnicity/SES represented proportionally?

items.title: Subgroup performance
items.body: Require performance data stratified by race, ethnicity, sex, age, and insurance status. Reject any vendor who cannot provide this. 'We don't have it' is an answer — and a red flag.

items.title: Local validation plan
items.body: Before go-live, commit to validating performance in your patient population. Build this into the contract — with a right to terminate if local validation fails.

items.title: Ongoing monitoring
items.body: Require contractual obligations for performance monitoring, bias reporting, and notification if the model is updated. Build internal monitoring into the deployment plan.

contentBlocks.heading: Build equity into the contract
contentBlocks.body: The best time to establish equity expectations is before signing the vendor contract. Include provisions requiring: (1) pre-deployment equity validation; (2) quarterly performance reports stratified by demographics; (3) notification of model updates; (4) right to audit model performance; (5) termination rights if equity performance degrades below agreed thresholds. Vendors who refuse these provisions are revealing something important.

questions.question: If an AI vendor cannot provide performance data stratified by race and ethnicity, how should a health system respond?
questions.explanation: The inability to provide subgroup performance data is a significant red flag — it means the vendor has not assessed whether their tool performs equitably. Health systems should treat this as a disqualifying factor, not a gap to be filled by trust.

options.text: Accept the tool and monitor for bias after deployment
Treat the inability to provide subgroup data as a significant red flag and consider disqualification
Ask the vendor to generate this data within 6 months of deployment
Accept FDA clearance as a substitute for subgroup performance data

tracks.title: Responsible AI Implementation
tracks.description: A practical framework for evaluating, procuring, deploying, and governing AI tools in health systems — from vendor assessment to post-deployment monitoring.

lessons.title: AI Governance: A Framework for Responsible Deployment
lessons.summary: A practical framework for health system AI governance — from pre-procurement evaluation through deployment, monitoring, and when to turn a model off.

objectives.text: Describe a pre-procurement AI evaluation framework
Identify the key elements of an AI monitoring program
Explain the criteria for deciding to turn off or retrain a deployed model

contentBlocks.heading: Most health systems are buying faster than they can govern
contentBlocks.body:
The AI market for healthcare is growing faster than health systems' capacity to evaluate what they buy. Vendors make dramatic claims; procurement teams rarely include clinical informaticists or equity experts; and post-deployment monitoring is the exception rather than the rule.

The consequence: health systems are deploying tools whose real-world performance is unknown, whose biases are uncharacterized, and whose failure modes are undocumented. This is a patient safety issue, not just a quality concern.

items.title: Problem definition
items.body: What clinical problem are you solving? What is the current standard of care? What would success look like — and how would you measure it?

items.title: Vendor evaluation
items.body: Request evidence of clinical validation in similar populations. Demand subgroup performance data. Ask about FDA status. Review published literature (not just vendor white papers).

items.title: Local validation
items.body: Before go-live, validate in your patient population. Compare model predictions to actual outcomes. Check performance by demographic subgroup.

items.title: Deployment design
items.body: Who sees the alert? When? What action do they take? Design the workflow around the model, not the model around the workflow. Plan for alert fatigue from day one.

items.title: Monitoring
items.body: Track model performance continuously — predictive accuracy, alert override rates, clinical outcomes. Set thresholds for when to escalate or retrain.

items.title: Retirement criteria
items.body: Pre-specify conditions under which you will retrain, pause, or retire the model — model drift, equity failures, patient harm signals, better alternatives.

contentBlocks.heading: The AHA/HIMSS AI governance principles
contentBlocks.body: The American Hospital Association and HIMSS have published AI governance principles for health systems covering: transparency (clinicians should know when AI is involved), explainability (clinicians should understand why a recommendation was made), equity (performance should be monitored by demographic subgroup), accountability (clear ownership of AI tools and their consequences), and safety (mechanisms to detect and respond to model failures).

contentBlocks.label: CMIO on building an AI governance committee
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a CMIO or Chief Digital Officer about how they built their health system's AI governance process — who is on the committee, what they evaluate, what they've rejected and why, and what they wish they had done earlier. Recommended: 10–12 minutes.

questions.question: What does 'local validation' mean in the AI implementation framework?
questions.explanation: Local validation means testing the model's performance in your own patient population before deployment — rather than relying solely on the vendor's validation studies, which may have been conducted in different populations.

options.text: Getting approval from your local institutional review board (IRB)
Testing model performance in your own patient population before go-live
Ensuring the model complies with your state's privacy laws
Reviewing the model's source code with your internal engineering team

lessons.title: Clinical Change Management for AI: Getting Clinicians to Use the Tool
lessons.summary: Why AI tools fail in deployment due to clinician resistance, workflow friction, and trust deficits — and the change management strategies that drive adoption.

objectives.text: Identify the primary reasons clinicians fail to adopt AI tools
Describe the role of physician champions in AI adoption
Apply change management principles to an AI implementation scenario

contentBlocks.heading: The last mile problem
contentBlocks.body:
Many health systems have procured, validated, and deployed AI tools that then sit largely unused. Clinicians click through alerts, ignore dashboards, or work around the tool entirely. This is the last mile problem: the technical challenge of building the AI is solved, but the human challenge of integrating it into clinical practice is not.

Studies of health IT adoption consistently find that workflow fit, trust, and perceived usefulness are the primary determinants of adoption — not technical performance. An AI tool that is 15% more accurate than a clinician but requires 30 additional seconds per patient will not be used.

items.title: Physician champions
items.body: Respected clinical leaders who use the tool and can explain it to peers. Champions provide social proof, answer clinical questions, and create pull instead of push for adoption.

items.title: Workflow co-design
items.body: Involve frontline clinicians in designing how the AI is integrated — where it appears, when it fires, what action it requests. Co-design creates ownership and catches implementation problems before go-live.

items.title: Transparent communication
items.body: Explain what the model does, what it doesn't do, and what its limitations are. Clinicians who understand a tool's boundaries use it more appropriately than those who see it as a black box.

items.title: Feedback loops
items.body: Show clinicians their own interaction with the tool — alert action rates, override patterns — and compare to peers. Behavioral feedback drives improvement without mandates.

contentBlocks.heading: The trust spectrum
contentBlocks.body: Clinician attitudes toward AI tools range from automation bias (over-trusting AI recommendations without applying clinical judgment) to automation skepticism (ignoring all AI output regardless of accuracy). Neither extreme serves patients well. Effective change management builds calibrated trust — clinicians who understand when to rely on the tool and when to override it, and who can do so confidently.

questions.question: What is 'automation bias' in the context of clinical AI adoption?
questions.explanation: Automation bias is the tendency to over-trust AI recommendations and apply them without appropriate clinical judgment — the opposite problem from ignoring AI entirely.

lessons.title: AI Ethics in Healthcare: Principles, Dilemmas & Accountability
lessons.summary: The ethical principles that should guide healthcare AI — beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy, justice — and how they play out in real clinical AI dilemmas.

objectives.text: Apply the four principles of bioethics to clinical AI scenarios
Explain the tension between transparency and performance in clinical AI
Describe what AI accountability means in practice for health systems

contentBlocks.heading: Bioethics meets machine learning
contentBlocks.body:
Clinical AI does not exist outside the ethical frameworks that govern all of medicine. The four principles of biomedical ethics — beneficence (do good), non-maleficence (do no harm), autonomy (respect patient choice), and justice (fair distribution of benefits and burdens) — apply as directly to an AI algorithm as they do to a surgical decision.

Applying these principles to AI reveals specific ethical challenges that don't arise in traditional clinical practice: Who is responsible when an AI recommendation causes harm? Does a patient have the right to know AI was involved in their care? Can a clinician ethically refuse to override an AI recommendation they disagree with?

items.title: Beneficence
items.body: AI must actually benefit patients — not just improve metrics. Deploying an AI that increases documentation speed but has unproven clinical benefit may not meet this standard.

items.title: Non-maleficence
items.body: AI systems can cause harm through false positives (unnecessary treatment), false negatives (missed diagnosis), algorithmic bias, and automation bias. Active harm monitoring is required.

items.title: Autonomy
items.body: Do patients have the right to know AI was involved in their care? Many argue yes — informed consent extends to AI tools, especially those making consequential recommendations.

items.title: Justice
items.body: AI must not worsen existing disparities. Systems that deploy AI tools with known bias in underserved populations are violating the justice principle — regardless of aggregate performance.

contentBlocks.heading: The explainability-performance tradeoff
contentBlocks.body: Deep learning models often outperform simpler, more explainable models (like logistic regression) — but their decisions cannot be explained in clinically meaningful terms. A sepsis model that says 'this patient has 73% risk' without explaining why creates an ethical challenge: clinicians are being asked to act on a recommendation they cannot evaluate. The field is developing explainability methods (SHAP, LIME, attention maps), but none yet provide the kind of clinical reasoning a physician can interrogate.

questions.question: Under the principle of autonomy, what is the emerging consensus about patient rights regarding clinical AI?
questions.explanation: The principle of autonomy — respecting patient decision-making — is increasingly interpreted to include the right to know when AI tools are involved in care decisions, as part of informed consent.

options.text: Patients have no right to know about AI use if the clinician reviews the recommendation
Patients should have the right to know when AI is involved in their care as part of informed consent
